nodes.label: Ventral tegmental area
nodes.rationale: Midline group of neurons on the midbrain floor; origin of dopaminergic cell bodies of the mesocorticolimbic system; implicated in reward cognition (motivational salience, associative learning, positively-valenced emotion) and orgasm; reciprocally connected with almost all of its projection targets.

nodes.label: Pars compacta
nodes.rationale: Supplies the striatum with dopamine; its main function, motor control, is indirect: excitatory D1-pathway input to the striatum disinhibits thalamocortical pathways to allow movement initiation. Loss of its neurons characterizes Parkinson's disease.

nodes.label: Pars reticulata
nodes.rationale: Mainly GABAergic, structurally and functionally similar to the internal globus pallidus; conveys final basal ganglia output to thalamus and superior colliculus; inhibits pars compacta dopaminergic activity via axon collaterals.

nodes.label: Substantia nigra
nodes.rationale: Basal ganglia structure in the midbrain (largest midbrain nucleus) with roles in reward and movement; 'black substance' because of neuromelanin in dopaminergic neurons; consists of pars compacta and pars reticulata.

nodes.label: Dopaminergic pathways
nodes.rationale: Sets of dopaminergic projection neurons involved in movement, cognition, executive function, reward, motivation and neuroendocrine control; more than 10 cell groups, four major pathways plus the hypothalamospinal and incertohypothalamic pathways.

nodes.label: Mesocortical pathway
nodes.rationale: VTA to prefrontal cortex; cognition and executive functions; dysregulation linked to ADHD.

nodes.label: Mesocorticolimbic system
nodes.rationale: Mesocortical plus mesolimbic pathways, both originating in the VTA; learning, motivation, reward, memory and movement; associated with ADHD, schizophrenia and addiction.

nodes.label: Mesolimbic pathway
nodes.rationale: The 'reward pathway' from VTA to ventral striatum (nucleus accumbens, olfactory tubercle); reward-related cognition, incentive salience ('wanting'), pleasure ('liking'), positive reinforcement and aversion; dopamine firing rises when reward is anticipated.

nodes.label: Dorsal striatum
nodes.rationale: Caudate nucleus and putamen; about 95% GABAergic medium spiny neurons and 5% cholinergic or GABAergic interneurons; receives glutamatergic input from all cortex, plus thalamus, hippocampus and amygdala.

nodes.label: Nigrostriatal pathway
nodes.rationale: Bilateral dopaminergic pathway from substantia nigra pars compacta to dorsal striatum; one of four major dopamine pathways; critical for movement via the basal ganglia motor loop and also influences cognition, reward and addiction; its degeneration underlies Parkinson's disease. Lateral SNc projects to lateral/caudal striatum, medial SNc to medial striatum.

nodes.label: Substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc)
nodes.rationale: Contains A9 dopaminergic neurons, about 200,000-420,000 in humans and 8,000-12,000 in mice; thin band overlying SNr, lateral to the VTA A10 group; neuromelanin-pigmented.

nodes.label: Mesocortical pathway
nodes.rationale: Dopaminergic pathway from ventral tegmentum to prefrontal cortex; one of four major dopamine pathways; essential to dorsolateral prefrontal cognitive function; involved in cognitive control, motivation and emotional response.

nodes.label: Tuberoinfundibular pathway
nodes.rationale: Dopamine neurons projecting from the arcuate (infundibular) nucleus of the tuberal hypothalamus to the median eminence; one of four major dopamine pathways; controls prolactin secretion.

nodes.norm_label: role in the central nervous system

nodes.label: Reward system
nodes.rationale: Evolved to increase adaptive fitness: it motivates approach to beneficial stimuli (sex, energy-dense food) by producing associative learning, approach/consummatory behavior and positively-valenced emotions.

nodes.label: Brainstem
nodes.rationale: Posterior stalk connecting cerebrum to spinal cord; only ~2.6% of brain weight yet critical for heart rate, breathing, sleep cycle and relaying motor/sensory pathways

nodes.label: Ascending reticular activating system
nodes.rationale: Acts as an on/off switch to the cerebral cortex, regulating wakefulness and sleep-wake transitions via several neurotransmitter arousal systems

nodes.label: Reticular formation
nodes.rationale: Phylogenetically old net of ~100 brainstem nuclei; modulatory functions sit in the rostral sector and premotor functions in caudal regions

nodes.label: Limbic system
nodes.rationale: Not an isolated emotion center but one of many regions regulating visceral autonomic processes, so the set of structures counted as limbic is controversial

nodes.label: Hypothalamus
nodes.rationale: Almond-sized basal diencephalon region whose key role is linking the nervous system to the endocrine system via the pituitary gland

nodes.label: Biological neuron model
nodes.rationale: Spiking neuron models describe how membrane potential changes over time; approaches range from realistic mechanistic models to pragmatic phenomenological ones, and the unusually large number of sometimes contradicting models stems from diverse experimental settings and the difficulty of separating intrinsic single-neuron properties from measurement and network effects.

nodes.label: Cable theory
nodes.rationale: Models passive dendrites and axons as cylinders of segments with membrane capacitance and resistance in parallel; capacitance arises from electrostatic forces across the thin lipid bilayer and series resistance from the axoplasm.

nodes.label: Length constant
nodes.rationale: lambda = sqrt(r_m / r_l): higher membrane resistance keeps current in the axoplasm so it travels farther; higher axoplasmic resistance shortens the distance.

nodes.label: Group A nerve fiber
nodes.rationale: Heavily myelinated class of nerve fiber found in both motor and sensory pathways; larger diameter axons and more myelin give faster propagation.

nodes.label: Group C nerve fiber
nodes.rationale: Unmyelinated, 0.2-1.5 um, conduction no more than 2 m/s; the lack of myelination is the cause of slow conduction.

nodes.label: Remak bundles
nodes.rationale: Non-myelinating Schwann cells bundle C fiber axons; bundles are thought to release trophic factors that promote regeneration of damaged axons.

nodes.label: Vanilloid receptor
nodes.rationale: TRPV1 responds to heat above 43 C, capsaicin and extracellular acidification, which is why chili peppers are sensed as hot.

nodes.label: Exponents reported by Stevens
nodes.rationale: The exponent a depends on modality, e.g. loudness 0.67, brightness 0.33, heaviness 1.45, electric shock 3.5.

nodes.label: Stevens's power law
nodes.rationale: psi(I) = k I^a; often considered to supersede the Weber–Fechner law because it describes a wider range of sensory comparisons, down to zero intensity.

nodes.label: Fechner's law
nodes.rationale: p = alpha ln(S/S0): geometric stimulus progressions map to arithmetic perception progressions; derived by assuming all JNDs are subjectively equal, an assumption later questioned.

nodes.label: Weber's law
nodes.rationale: The just-noticeable difference is proportional to the initial stimulus (dS_JND = kS); the brain detects relative, not absolute, change. It fails at low intensities and often at high ones.

nodes.label: Sensory neuron
nodes.rationale: Predominantly pseudounipolar or bipolar in vertebrates; converts a stimulus via its receptors into action potentials or graded receptor potentials.

nodes.label: Spinal nerve
nodes.rationale: 31 pairs of mixed nerves (8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal) carrying motor, sensory and autonomic signals between spinal cord and body.

nodes.label: Cranial nerves
nodes.rationale: Nerves emerging directly from the brain and brainstem above the atlas, conventionally twelve pairs (I-XII) plus the terminal nerve (0).

nodes.label: Autonomic nervous system
nodes.rationale: Self-regulating, involuntary control of smooth muscle, glands, heart rate and digestion.

nodes.label: Peripheral nervous system
nodes.rationale: Nerves and ganglia outside brain and spinal cord relaying between CNS and body; more vulnerable than the CNS because it lacks protection of the vertebral column, skull and blood-brain barrier.

nodes.label: Reflex arcs
nodes.rationale: Neural circuit giving a near-automatic link from sensory input to motor output; simplest is two-element monosynaptic, next is three-element via spinal interneurons.

nodes.label: Somatic nervous system
nodes.rationale: Voluntary nervous system linking brain and spinal cord to skeletal muscles and skin receptors; 43 nerve segments (31 spinal, 12 brainstem), each with a sensory and motor pair.

nodes.label: Brachial plexus
nodes.rationale: Nerve plexus from anterior rami of C5-T1 running through the cervicoaxillary canal into the axilla, supplying chest, shoulder, arm, forearm and hand.

nodes.label: Phrenic nerve
nodes.rationale: Because the phrenic nerve arises high in the neck (C3-C5) yet innervates the much lower diaphragm, spinal cord injuries below the neck spare breathing; it must be identified and preserved during thoracic surgery.

nodes.label: Hypothalamus
nodes.rationale: Receives electrical signals from many brain regions and translates them into chemical signals (hormones or releasing factors).

nodes.label: Sympathoadrenal system
nodes.rationale: Article is flagged (September 2025) for conflating SAM, SNS and HPA terminology and relying on outdated sources; stress-section claims warrant caution.

nodes.label: Hippocampus
nodes.rationale: Neuronal cell types are neatly organized into layers, so it is frequently used as a model system for studying neurophysiology

nodes.label: Insular cortex
nodes.rationale: Higher-level functions such as empathy and metacognitive feelings are thought not to be distinct from the insula's lower-level functions but to arise from its role in conveying homeostatic information to consciousness.

nodes.label: Neuromodulation
nodes.rationale: Neuromodulators act via metabotropic GPCRs and second messengers, giving broad, long-lasting signals (hundreds of ms to minutes); a neuromodulator behaves like a neurotransmitter that is not reabsorbed or broken down, so it can linger in CSF and influence many neurons.

nodes.label: Neuromodulator systems
nodes.rationale: Drugs targeting the transmitter of one of these systems affect the whole system, which explains the mode of action of many drugs.

nodes.label: Nomenclature
nodes.rationale: Latin names like 'nucleus raphe magnus' are grammatically incorrect; Terminologia Anatomica uses the genitive 'raphes', and some sources argue 'rhaphe' is the correct rendering of the Greek word.

nodes.label: Sleep and arousal regulation
nodes.rationale: Raphe lesions cause insomnia yet serotonergic firing rises in wakefulness; one resolution is that waking serotonin release triggers genomic events in preoptic sleep-promoting neurons that later raise sleep propensity.

nodes.label: Large-scale brain network
nodes.rationale: There is no universal network atlas because networks vary with resolution, spatial and time scale, individuals, and dynamics; WHATNET was formed to reach consensus nomenclature.

nodes.label: Neuron
nodes.rationale: Electrically excitable cell that fires action potentials and communicates with other cells via synapses using neurotransmitters; primary signaling unit of the nervous system.

nodes.label: Action potential
nodes.rationale: Rapid, stereotyped rise and fall of membrane potential (nerve impulse/spike) produced by voltage-gated ion channels; propagates along the axon toward synaptic boutons.

nodes.label: Nerve conduction velocity
nodes.rationale: Speed of electrochemical impulse propagation along a neural pathway (about 0.5 to over 120 m/s); depends largely on axon diameter and degree of myelination.

nodes.label: Myelin
nodes.rationale: Lipid-rich insulating sheath around axons that increases action potential speed; lowers membrane capacitance and raises resistance; suggested to permit larger body size by keeping distant body parts in fast communication.

nodes.label: Synapse
nodes.rationale: Structure letting a neuron exchange signals with an adjacent cell; a junction for both transmission and processing of information.

nodes.label: Neurotransmitter
nodes.rationale: Signaling molecule secreted by a neuron to affect a target cell across a synapse; its effect is determined by the receptor it binds; more than 100 identified in humans.

nodes.label: Retina
nodes.rationale: Originates as an outgrowth of the embryonic diencephalon, so it is considered CNS brain tissue; the only nervous tissue visible noninvasively and the body part with the greatest continuous energy demand. Functions like a camera image sensor.

nodes.label: Cochlea
nodes.rationale: Spiral cavity of the bony labyrinth (2.75 turns around the modiolus) that transduces sound vibrations into neural signals for hearing.

nodes.label: Mechanoreceptor
nodes.rationale: Sensory receptor on sensory neurons that converts mechanical pressure or distortion into action potentials sent to the CNS.

nodes.label: Nociception
nodes.rationale: Sensory nervous system process of encoding noxious stimuli to trigger defensive responses; usually but not necessarily yields pain perception.

nodes.label: Pain
nodes.rationale: Distressing sensory and emotional experience tied to actual or potential tissue damage; motivates withdrawal, protection of injured parts, and future avoidance.

nodes.label: Semicircular canal system
nodes.rationale: Each canal has a near-parallel contralateral partner that is inhibited when it is excited, so the pair can sense all directions of rotation; vertical canals couple in a crossed fashion.

nodes.label: Sweetness
nodes.rationale: Sweet taste signals carbohydrates in solution; carbohydrates are calorie-dense, so the human body evolved to seek out high-calorie foods.

nodes.label: Interoception
nodes.rationale: An integrated, highly accurate representation of the body's physiological state is important for maintaining homeostasis and may facilitate self-awareness; misrepresentation of internal signals is proposed to underlie several psychiatric conditions.

nodes.label: Dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway
nodes.rationale: Major sensory pathway of the CNS for fine touch, vibration, two-point discrimination and proprioception; all its axons are rapidly conducting, large, myelinated fibers, and it decussates in the medulla.

nodes.label: Quantal transmission
nodes.rationale: Exocytosis releases ACh in packets (quanta) of 7000-10,000 molecules; each quantum reaches the endplate at millimolar concentration, enough to bind low-affinity receptors that swiftly release the transmitter, which makes nerve-to-muscle transmission very rapid.

nodes.label: Withdrawal reflex
nodes.rationale: Polysynaptic spinal reflex that protects the body from damaging stimuli by contracting flexors and relaxing extensors of the limb.

nodes.label: Stretch reflex
nodes.rationale: Muscle contraction resisting stretch, generally to maintain constant muscle length; the older term 'deep tendon reflex' is criticized as misleading because muscle spindles, not tendons, detect the stretch.

nodes.label: Central pattern generator
nodes.rationale: Self-organizing neural circuit producing rhythmic output without rhythmic input; requires interacting processes that sequentially rise and fall so the system repeatedly returns to its start; still needs modulatory input and stays flexible to sensory feedback.

nodes.label: Autonomic nervous system
nodes.rationale: Largely unconscious control system for viscera, smooth muscle and glands (heart rate, digestion, respiration, pupillary response, urination, sexual arousal).

nodes.label: Sympathetic nervous system
nodes.rationale: Primary process is the fight-or-flight response but it is tonically active to maintain homeostasis; antagonistic to the parasympathetic system.

nodes.label: Parasympathetic nervous system
nodes.rationale: Promotes energy conservation, metabolic storage and long-timescale homeostasis, complementary to the sympathetic system that predominates in acute stress.

nodes.label: Vagus nerve
nodes.rationale: Longest autonomic nerve, mostly sensory; historically called the pneumogastric nerve for lung and gut roles, though its cardiac regulation is fundamental.

nodes.label: Sympathetic trunk
nodes.rationale: Lets preganglionic sympathetic fibers ascend above T1 and descend below L2/3, so fibers can reach spinal nerves superior and inferior to the level where they originated.

nodes.label: Baroreflex
nodes.rationale: A rapid negative feedback loop that acts within one cardiac cycle, which makes it key for countering postural (orthostatic) hypotension; slower ANP and renin-angiotensin systems complement it. Coupling sympathetic inhibition with parasympathetic activation maximizes blood pressure correction.

nodes.label: Fight-or-flight response
nodes.rationale: Its physiological changes give the body more strength and speed ahead of fighting or running: glucose release, blood shifted to muscles and brain, faster breathing, faster clotting and dilated pupils. Researchers moved to the terms 'hyperarousal' or 'acute stress response' because observed responses also include freezing, flop, faint and fawn.

nodes.label: Thermoregulation
nodes.rationale: Dormancy, torpor and a lower metabolic rate in the cold shrink the temperature gap between body and air and cost less energy, so they conserve energy. Endotherms carry more mitochondria per cell, which lets them make more metabolic heat.

nodes.label: Respiratory center
nodes.rationale: Breathing has to keep going on its own during sleep, so rhythm generation belongs to the autonomic nervous system. The center combines chemoreceptor, mechanoreceptor, cortical and hypothalamic input to adjust the rate and depth of breathing homeostatically.

nodes.label: Heart rate
nodes.rationale: With no nervous input the SA node would fire at about 100 bpm. Resting rates are lower, so vagal (parasympathetic) stimulation dominates at rest, like driving with one foot on the brake. Rates above about 100 bpm need sympathetic stimulation.

nodes.label: Pelvic splanchnic nerves
nodes.rationale: Sacral (S2-S4) parasympathetic outflow to pelvic organs; distal colon and rectum get parasympathetic supply here while proximal gut is supplied by the vagus nerve.

nodes.label: Enteric nervous system
nodes.rationale: Called the 'second brain' because it has ~500 million neurons, afferent/efferent/interneurons that run reflexes without CNS input, >30 CNS-like neurotransmitters, astroglia-like support cells and a BBB-like barrier.

nodes.label: Myenteric plexus
nodes.rationale: Major nerve supply to the GI tract; provides motor innervation to both muscle layers and controls GI motility, with ~30% of its neurons being sensory.

nodes.label: Inflammatory reflex
nodes.rationale: Neural circuit whose efferent vagal signaling inhibits inflammation and prevents organ damage from excessive cytokine production.

nodes.label: Neuroimmune system
nodes.rationale: Protects neurons by maintaining selectively permeable barriers, mediating neuroinflammation and wound healing, and mobilizing host defences against pathogens.

nodes.label: Sickness behavior
nodes.rationale: A coordinated adaptive motivational state that reorganizes priorities to cope with infection; reduced activity diverts metabolic energy to fever and limits predator exposure.

nodes.label: Fever
nodes.rationale: Fever evolved as an anti-infection defense mechanism, yet treating fever does not appear to improve or worsen outcomes.

nodes.label: Hyperthermia
nodes.rationale: Distinguished clinically from fever because the set point is unchanged, it can quickly be fatal and it does not respond to antipyretics.

nodes.label: Spinal cord injury
nodes.rationale: Damage to the spinal cord causing temporary or permanent motor, sensory and autonomic dysfunction; mostly from physical trauma, just over half affect the cervical spine.

nodes.label: Vagotomy
nodes.rationale: Surgical removal of part of the vagus nerve in the abdomen; once standard for peptic ulcer disease but largely displaced by H2 blockers, PPIs and H. pylori eradication.

nodes.label: Sympathectomy
nodes.rationale: Irreversible procedure in which at least one sympathetic ganglion is removed.

nodes.label: Dysautonomia
nodes.rationale: Malfunction of the autonomic nervous system affecting heart, bladder, intestines, sweat glands, pupils and blood vessels; diagnosed by functional ANS testing and treated symptomatically, ranging from transient to life-threatening.

nodes.rationale: Orgasms within a short period of one another; possible, especially in women, but uncommon.

nodes.label: Oxytocin

nodes.label: Clitoris
nodes.rationale: More than 8,000 sensory nerve endings; homologous to the penis; 70-80 percent of women require direct clitoral stimulation to reach orgasm.

nodes.label: Extended or Continuous Orgasm
nodes.rationale: Debated classification: subjective sensations lasting minutes to an hour, felt throughout the body, without the characteristic involuntary contractions.

nodes.label: Vaginal Nerve Ending Distribution
nodes.rationale: Vagina has far fewer nerve endings than the clitoris; densest at the lower third near the entrance; anterior wall areas are especially sensitive.

nodes.label: Prolactin
nodes.rationale: Neurohormone released after orgasm, contributing to post-orgasmic relaxation.

nodes.label: Endorphins
nodes.rationale: Endogenous morphine released after orgasm.

nodes.label: Resolution Phase
nodes.rationale: Post-orgasm period, typically relaxing because of the release of oxytocin, prolactin and endorphins.

nodes.label: Clinical Definition of Orgasm
nodes.rationale: Defined by muscular contractions plus characteristic heart rate, blood pressure, respiration rate and depth changes; at least 26 definitions exist; physiological, psychological, endocrinological and neurological definitions differ.

nodes.label: Mah and Binik (2001), Clinical Psychology Review
nodes.norm_label: mah and binik (2001), clinical psychology review
nodes.rationale: Lists at least 26 definitions of orgasm.

nodes.label: Cerebral Cortex Metabolic Decrease
nodes.rationale: Temporary decrease in metabolic activity of large parts of the cerebral cortex during orgasm.

nodes.label: Ejaculation
nodes.rationale: Usually accompanies male orgasm, but modern findings support a distinction between ejaculation and male orgasm.

nodes.label: Limbic System Activity
nodes.rationale: No change or increased metabolic activity in limbic areas while the cortex quiets.

nodes.label: Muscular Spasms, Body Movements and Vocalizations

nodes.label: Orgasm
nodes.rationale: Sudden release of accumulated sexual excitement during the sexual response cycle; intense pleasure with rhythmic, involuntary pelvic muscle contractions; controlled by the autonomic nervous system; experienced by both sexes.

nodes.label: Psychogenic Orgasm
nodes.rationale: Orgasm can be reached through psychological arousal alone (dreams, reports from people with spinal cord injury); physical stimulation is not a requisite, but a suitable psychological state is.

nodes.label: Vance and Wagner (1976) Orgasm Description Study
nodes.norm_label: vance and wagner (1976) orgasm description study
nodes.rationale: Independent raters could not differentiate written descriptions of male versus female orgasm.

nodes.label: Human Sexual Response Cycle
nodes.rationale: Four-stage model of physiological responses to sexual stimulation: excitement, plateau, orgasm, resolution; first formulated by Masters and Johnson in 1966; later criticized and supplemented by other models.

nodes.label: Orgasm Phase
nodes.rationale: Ends the plateau phase; quick cycles of lower pelvic muscle contraction, involuntary vocalizations and spasms, euphoria; heart rate rises further.

nodes.label: Orgasmic Platform
nodes.rationale: Masters and Johnson term for plateau-stage changes: outer third of the vagina swells and the pubococcygeus muscle tightens.

nodes.label: Plateau Phase
nodes.rationale: Period before orgasm: increased circulation, heart rate, pleasure and muscle tension; respiration stays elevated.

nodes.label: Resolution Phase
nodes.rationale: Muscles relax, blood pressure drops and the body slows from its excited state.

nodes.label: Ejaculation
nodes.rationale: First and second convulsions are the most intense; each later contraction carries less semen and milder pleasure.

nodes.label: Heart Rate, Breathing and Blood Pressure Rise
nodes.norm_label: heart rate, breathing and blood pressure rise

nodes.label: Excitement Phase
nodes.rationale: First stage, triggered by physical or mental erotic stimuli; heart rate, breathing and blood pressure rise; myotonia begins; in females lasts minutes to hours.

nodes.label: Myotonia
nodes.rationale: Increase in muscle tone of certain muscle groups, voluntary and involuntary, beginning in the excitement phase.

nodes.label: Sex Flush
nodes.rationale: Skin vasocongestion in about 50-75% of females and 25% of males; more common in warm conditions; fades after orgasm (up to two hours) in reverse order of appearance.

nodes.label: Vasocongestion
nodes.rationale: Swells clitoris, labia minora and vagina and darkens clitoris and vaginal walls during arousal.

nodes.label: 2006 Nipple Stimulation Arousal Survey
nodes.rationale: Arousal arises or is enhanced by nipple stimulation in about 82% of young females and 52% of young males.

nodes.label: Rutgers University 1995 Multiple Orgasm Study
nodes.rationale: Six fully ejaculatory orgasms in 36 minutes with no apparent refractory period.

nodes.label: Oxytocin
nodes.rationale: Increased infusion during ejaculation is believed chiefly responsible for the male refractory period; the size of the increase may set its length.

nodes.label: 2023 Gender-Affirming Hormone Therapy Orgasm Study
nodes.rationale: 130 transgender women and 33 transgender men; many shifted from short single-peak to longer multiple-peak orgasms.

nodes.label: Age Dependence of Refractory Period
nodes.rationale: About 15 minutes at age 18 versus about 20 hours in the 70s; rare males show under 10 seconds.

nodes.label: Peripheral Autonomic Feedback Theory
nodes.rationale: After ejaculation, lower seminal vesicle wall tension alters autonomic signals and forms a negative feedback loop that holds until wall tension is restored; restoration slows with age (citation needed).

nodes.label: Female Refractory Period
nodes.rationale: Contested: some sources say females lack one, others that most experience one; most women report clitoral hypersensitivity after orgasm at rates similar to men.

nodes.label: Gonadotropin-Inhibitory Hormone (GnIH)
nodes.rationale: Proposed to cause post-ejaculatory refractoriness by inhibiting the HPG axis and sexual functions.

nodes.label: Post-Orgasmic Genital Hypersensitivity
nodes.rationale: Penis or clitoris may be hypersensitive; further stimulation can feel painful or uncomfortable.

nodes.label: Prolactin
nodes.rationale: Proposed cause of the refractory period; repressed by dopamine; elevated for about 60 minutes after orgasm in both sexes; causal role lacks consensus.

nodes.label: Refractory Period
nodes.rationale: Recovery phase after orgasm during which further orgasm is physiologically impossible; in males begins immediately after ejaculation and lasts until the excitement phase begins anew; ranges from minutes to days.

nodes.norm_label: rosenthal (2012) human sexuality: from cells to society

nodes.label: Sexual Arousal
nodes.rationale: Physiological and psychological responses in preparation for sexual intercourse or to sexual stimuli; with sufficient stimulation it intensifies and can precipitate orgasm.

nodes.label: McGill Thermal Imaging Arousal Study
nodes.rationale: Genital temperature imaging showed men and women reach peak arousal in about 10 minutes on average.

nodes.label: Erotic Stimuli
nodes.rationale: Classified by sense: somatosensory, visual and olfactory, with auditory stimuli secondary.

nodes.label: Arousal Non-Concordance
nodes.rationale: Erection and subjective arousal are not one-to-one.

nodes.label: Male Sex Flush Spread Pattern
nodes.rationale: Less consistent; starts at the epigastrium, spreads across the chest to neck, face, forehead, back and sometimes shoulders and forearms.

nodes.label: Sex Flush

nodes.label: Ambient Temperature Dependence of Sex Flush
nodes.norm_label: ambient temperature dependence of sex flush

nodes.label: Post-Orgasmic Flush Fading

nodes.label: Blushing

nodes.label: Unrelieved Sexual Vasocongestion Pain
nodes.rationale: Sex-related vasocongestion without sexual release can cause cramp-like pain in males ('blue balls') and pelvic heaviness in women.

nodes.label: Vasocongestion
nodes.rationale: Swelling of bodily tissues from increased vascular blood flow and a localized rise in blood pressure; caused by menstruation, sexual arousal, REM sleep, strong emotions, illness, deep venous thrombosis and allergic reactions.

nodes.label: Oxytocin
nodes.rationale: Peptide hormone/neuropeptide made in the hypothalamus and released by the posterior pituitary; released into the bloodstream in response to sexual activity and during childbirth. Nicknamed the love/cuddle hormone because of its involvement in mating and social behavior. Elimination half-life 1-6 min IV, about 2 h intranasal - a fast pulse-like signal.

nodes.label: Vincent du Vigneaud
nodes.rationale: Sequenced and in 1953 synthesized oxytocin, the first polypeptide hormone to be sequenced and synthesized; Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1955.

nodes.label: Oxytocin Positive Feedback Release
nodes.rationale: Initial oxytocin release stimulates production and release of more oxytocin, increasing intensity and frequency of contractions; the loop intensifies until the triggering activity ceases. The same self-amplifying process occurs during lactation and sexual activity - a natural model for an escalating climax that collapses once the stimulus stops.

nodes.label: Prolactin
nodes.rationale: Peptide hormone (lactotropin/mammotropin) secreted by the pituitary gland, influential in over 300 processes including lactation, metabolism and immune regulation. The captured page is truncated mid-sentence in the hypothalamic-regulation paragraph, so dopamine-inhibition control and any post-orgasmic role are not covered by this source.

nodes.label: Cytokine-like Signaling
nodes.rationale: Prolactin acts in endocrine, autocrine and paracrine manners through the prolactin receptor and numerous cytokine receptors.

nodes.label: Addictive Drugs (Cocaine, Amphetamine, Alcohol, Nicotine, Opiates)
nodes.norm_label: addictive drugs (cocaine, amphetamine, alcohol, nicotine, opiates)

nodes.label: Medial Forebrain Bundle
nodes.rationale: Route of ipsilateral SNc dopamine axons to the dorsal striatum.

nodes.label: Prefrontal Cortex
nodes.rationale: Target of the mesocortical pathway and a glutamatergic input back to the VTA.

nodes.label: Olfactory Tubercle
nodes.rationale: With 27 inputs and 20 outputs it verifies odor signals, regulates odor-driven social motor behavior, integrates auditory and olfactory input, and relays positive signals to reward circuits (implicated in addiction).

nodes.label: Mesolimbic Pathway (Reward Pathway)
nodes.rationale: Dopaminergic projection from the VTA to the ventral striatum. Neuron firing rises during anticipation of reward (craving); dopamine release here was once considered the main mediator of pleasure but is now believed to play only a minor or secondary role - it drives wanting (incentive salience) more than liking.

nodes.label: Medial Dorsal Nucleus of the Thalamus
nodes.norm_label: medial dorsal nucleus of the thalamus

nodes.label: Nucleus Accumbens Shell
nodes.rationale: Outer region; part of the extended amygdala; holds most mixed D1/D2 medium spiny neurons; fewer dendritic spines than the core.

nodes.label: Nucleus Accumbens (NAcc)
nodes.rationale: Basal forebrain region forming the ventral striatum with the olfactory tubercle; processes motivation, aversion, reward (incentive salience, pleasure, positive reinforcement) and reinforcement learning. Its GABAergic neurons are activated by rewarding experiences such as sex, music and exercise.

nodes.label: Descending Pain Modulation
nodes.rationale: PAG stimulation activates enkephalin neurons projecting to the raphe nuclei; serotonin descends to dorsal-horn inhibitory interneurons that release enkephalin/dynorphin onto opioid receptors, blocking nociceptive transmission before it reaches cortex. Electrical PAG stimulation gives immediate, profound analgesia.

nodes.label: Orbitofrontal Cortex
nodes.rationale: Lateral OFC responds to pleasant visual, tactile and olfactory stimuli according to pleasantness rather than intensity.

nodes.label: Spinothalamic Tract
nodes.rationale: Main pathway for pain and temperature perception; it crosses the spinal cord immediately, which helps localize injury clinically.

nodes.label: Deep Brain Stimulation for Chronic Pain
nodes.norm_label: deep brain stimulation for chronic pain

nodes.label: Defensive Behavior (Dorsal/Lateral PAG)
nodes.rationale: Stimulation of dorsal/lateral PAG provokes freezing, running, jumping, tachycardia and increased blood pressure and muscle tonus.

nodes.label: Periaqueductal Gray (PAG)
nodes.rationale: Midbrain gray matter around the cerebral aqueduct; critical for autonomic function, motivated behavior, responses to threat, and the primary control center for descending pain modulation via enkephalin-producing cells.

nodes.label: Quiescence (Caudal Ventrolateral PAG)
nodes.rationale: Stimulation of caudal ventrolateral PAG produces an immobile, relaxed posture; its inhibition increases locomotor activity.

nodes.label: Vocal Production Gating
nodes.rationale: PAG initiates and gates species-typical vocalizations; lesions abolish vocal output without disrupting other motor behaviors, so it enables vocalization rather than shaping acoustic structure.

nodes.label: Basbaum and Fields 1978 - Endogenous Pain Control Mechanisms
nodes.norm_label: basbaum and fields 1978 - endogenous pain control mechanisms

nodes.label: Faull et al. 2019 - PAG as Integrative Interoceptive Structure for Breathing
nodes.norm_label: faull et al. 2019 - pag as integrative interoceptive structure for breathing

nodes.label: Silva and McNaughton 2019 - PAG and Dorsal Raphe in Appetitive and Aversive Control
nodes.norm_label: silva and mcnaughton 2019 - pag and dorsal raphe in appetitive and aversive control

nodes.label: Peripheral paracrine dopamine signaling
nodes.rationale: Outside the CNS dopamine is synthesized locally and acts near the cells that release it (blood vessels excepted).

nodes.label: Reward anticipation raises dopamine
nodes.rationale: Anticipation of most types of rewards increases the level of dopamine in the brain; addictive drugs increase release or block reuptake.

nodes.label: Motivational salience
nodes.rationale: Current pharmacology view: dopamine is not the chemical of pleasure but signals the motivational prominence (desirability or aversiveness) of an outcome, directing behavior toward or away from it.

nodes.label: Cocaine
nodes.rationale: Blocks the dopamine transporter so dopamine lingers in the synaptic cleft and keeps activating receptors.

nodes.label: Lateral habenula
nodes.rationale: Inhibits VTA dopamine neurons by exciting RMTg GABAergic neurons; thought to be important for reward prediction errors; also a glutamatergic input to the VTA.

nodes.label: Lateral hypothalamus
nodes.rationale: Provides both glutamatergic and GABAergic afferents to the VTA.

nodes.label: Mesohabenular pathway
nodes.rationale: Rodent VTA neurons projecting to the habenula that release glutamate and GABA rather than dopamine.

nodes.label: Nucleus accumbens
nodes.rationale: Main target of the mesolimbic pathway and also a GABAergic input back to the VTA.

nodes.label: Parabrachial pigmented area (PBP)
nodes.rationale: Dopamine-rich VTA subdivision of medium-to-large, moderately staining TH-positive cell bodies.

nodes.label: Parafasciculus retroflexus area (PFR)
nodes.rationale: VTA subdivision with a low density of small, lightly staining TH-positive cells.

nodes.label: Paranigral nucleus (PN)
nodes.rationale: Dopamine-rich VTA subdivision of medium-to-large, moderately staining TH-positive cell bodies.

nodes.label: Rostromedial tegmental nucleus (RMTg, tail of VTA)
nodes.norm_label: rostromedial tegmental nucleus (rmtg, tail of vta)
nodes.rationale: Mostly GABAergic; its GABAergic afferents to the VTA act as a 'master brake' on VTA dopamine pathways; excited by the lateral habenula.

nodes.label: Ventral pallidum (subpallidal area)
nodes.rationale: Substantial subpallidal GABAergic pathway to the VTA; its disinhibition increases mesolimbic dopamine release and amplifies locomotor activity.

nodes.label: Cholinergic inputs to VTA
nodes.rationale: From PPTg and laterodorsal tegmental nucleus; optogenetic studies in mice show they reinforce the discharge properties of VTA neurons, a modulatory influence on reward circuits.

nodes.label: GABAergic afferents to VTA
nodes.rationale: Arise from nucleus accumbens, ventral pallidum, dorsal raphe, lateral hypothalamus, periaqueductal gray, BNST and RMTg; subpallidal afferents are mainly inhibitory. Because VTA neurons are heterogeneous, glutamatergic and GABAergic inputs are not exclusively excitatory or inhibitory.

nodes.label: Glutamatergic afferents to VTA
nodes.rationale: Arise from prefrontal cortex, PPTg, laterodorsal tegmental nucleus, subthalamic nucleus, BNST, superior colliculus, periaqueductal gray, lateral habenula, dorsal raphe, lateral hypothalamus and preoptic area; activation raises dopamine neuron firing rate and induces burst firing; critical to effects of drugs of abuse.

nodes.label: Dopaminergic cell group A10
nodes.rationale: VTA cells are designated A10 because of their selective limbic-related afferents.

nodes.label: Dopamine neuron burst firing
nodes.rationale: Glutamatergic drive increases VTA dopamine neuron firing rate and switches neurons into burst firing, the phasic mode behind peak dopamine release.

nodes.label: Preoptic area
nodes.rationale: Source of glutamatergic afferents to the VTA.

nodes.label: Neuromelanin
nodes.rationale: Dark pigment in dopaminergic neurons that accumulates with age and makes the SNc visible in brain sections.

nodes.label: Nigrothalamic pathway
nodes.rationale: GABAergic projections from pars reticulata to ventral lateral and ventral anterior thalamus, superior colliculus and other caudal nuclei.

nodes.label: Direct pathway (basal ganglia)
nodes.rationale: Axons of striatal medium spiny cells project directly to the pars reticulata, inhibiting it.

nodes.label: Indirect pathway (basal ganglia)
nodes.rationale: Striatum to external globus pallidus to subthalamic nucleus (glutamatergic) to pars reticulata; net excitatory effect on SNpr.

nodes.label: Parkinson's disease
nodes.rationale: Characterized by loss of SNpc dopaminergic neurons, producing hypokinesia, tremor, rigidity and postural imbalance; also shows altered pars reticulata firing patterns.

nodes.label: Subthalamic nucleus
nodes.rationale: Glutamatergic input that modulates pars reticulata firing; its lesion lowers SNpr firing by only about 20%.

nodes.label: Pars reticulata spontaneous firing (~25 Hz)
nodes.rationale: SNpr GABAergic neurons fire action potentials autonomously at roughly 25 Hz (rats) to tonically inhibit basal ganglia targets; decreases in this inhibition accompany movement; single-spike or burst patterns appear in Parkinson's disease and epilepsy.

nodes.label: Tyrosine hydroxylase
nodes.rationale: Enzyme required for dopamine synthesis; TH-positive staining marks dopaminergic cells.

nodes.label: Executive functions
nodes.rationale: Attention, working memory, inhibitory control and planning, regulated by the mesocortical pathway.

nodes.label: Hypothalamospinal tract
nodes.rationale: Hypothalamus to spinal cord; influences brainstem and spinal locomotor networks; associated with restless legs syndrome.

nodes.label: Incertohypothalamic pathway
nodes.rationale: Zona incerta to hypothalamus and brainstem locomotor centers; visceral and sensorimotor activities; associated with tremor.

nodes.label: Dopamine synthesis, storage and release
nodes.rationale: TH and DOPA decarboxylase are produced in the soma; dopamine is stored in the cytoplasm and in axon-terminal vesicles; vesicular release is triggered by action-potential-induced membrane depolarization; axons extend the full length of the pathway.

nodes.label: Dopaminergic cell groups
nodes.rationale: More than 10 dopaminergic cell groups exist in the brain.

nodes.label: D1/D2 complementary learning from positive and negative feedback
nodes.norm_label: d1/d2 complementary learning from positive and negative feedback
nodes.rationale: D1 and D2 receptor subtypes have complementary functions in the mesocorticolimbic projection, facilitating learning from both positive and negative feedback.

nodes.label: Reward anticipation increases dopamine firing
nodes.rationale: When a reward is anticipated, the firing rate of mesolimbic dopamine neurons increases.

nodes.label: Caudate nucleus
nodes.rationale: Receives input largely from association cortex.

nodes.label: Medium spiny neurons (MSNs / SPNs)
nodes.rationale: GABAergic striatal projection neurons; about half express D1 receptors (direct pathway) and half D2 receptors (indirect pathway).

nodes.label: Putamen
nodes.rationale: Receives input largely from sensorimotor cortex.

nodes.label: Striosome (patch) and matrix compartments
nodes.rationale: Striosomes show dense mu-opioid receptor staining; the surrounding matrix has higher acetylcholinesterase and calbindin-D28K.

nodes.label: Dopamine neuron axonal arborization
nodes.rationale: Each nigrostriatal dopamine neuron has an extremely large unmyelinated arbor innervating up to 6% of rat striatal volume, with collaterals to pedunculopontine nucleus, ventral pallidum, subthalamic nucleus, globus pallidus, amygdala and thalamus.

nodes.label: Dopamine-glutamate dendritic spine synapse
nodes.rationale: Nigrostriatal terminals synapse mostly on the necks of MSN dendritic spines whose heads receive glutamatergic input, so dopamine modulates cortical input at the same spine.

nodes.label: GABA co-release by dopamine axons
nodes.rationale: Some nigrostriatal axons co-release GABA along with dopamine.

nodes.label: SNc dorsal and ventral tiers
nodes.rationale: Dorsal-tier dopamine cells contain calbindin-D28K that buffers calcium, have horizontal dendrites and project mostly to the matrix and ventromedial striatum; ventral-tier cells lack calbindin, are more vulnerable to neurotoxins such as MPTP, extend dendrites into the SNr and project mostly to striosomes and dorsal caudate/putamen.

nodes.label: Tonic and phasic dopamine firing
nodes.rationale: Nigrostriatal dopamine neurons show tonic and phasic firing patterns that yield different patterns of dopamine release from striatal axon terminals and from soma/dendrites in SNc and SNr; the two-mode basis for dopamine dynamics models.

nodes.label: Psychostimulants (methylphenidate, amphetamine)
nodes.rationale: Low therapeutic doses improve working memory in ADHD and normal subjects by triggering dopamine and norepinephrine release via plasma membrane transporters and VMAT; high abused doses impair working memory and cognitive control; D1 agonist/antagonist studies support the dopamine role.

nodes.label: Hypophyseal portal system
nodes.rationale: Portal capillaries deliver factors released by hypothalamic neurons at the median eminence to the anterior pituitary.

nodes.label: Antipsychotic drugs
nodes.rationale: Some block dopamine in the tuberoinfundibular pathway, raising blood prolactin.

nodes.label: Dopamine-mediated prolactin inhibition
nodes.rationale: Dopamine released at the median eminence binds D2 receptors on anterior pituitary lactotrophs and inhibits prolactin secretion; blocking it raises blood prolactin.

nodes.label: Beta-arrestin

nodes.label: Dopamine receptor abundance ordering
nodes.rationale: Relative abundance is D1 > D2 > D3 > D5 > D4; D1-D2 subtypes occur at 10-100 times the levels of D3-D5, so D1/D2 dominate population-level dopamine signaling.

nodes.label: AMPA/NMDA current potentiation
nodes.rationale: DARPP-32 mediated PP1 inhibition amplifies PKA phosphorylation of AMPA, NMDA and inward rectifying potassium channels, raising AMPA/NMDA currents and lowering potassium conductance.

nodes.label: Extrinsic rewards
nodes.rationale: Extrinsic rewards are not inherently pleasurable; they derive motivational value from learned association (conditioning) with intrinsic rewards.

nodes.label: Medium spiny neurons (MSNs)
nodes.rationale: Principal GABAergic inhibitory neurons, about 95% of human striatal neurons; about 40% co-express DRD1 and DRD2 mRNA.

nodes.label: Striatum
nodes.rationale: Largest component; receives input from many brain areas but sends output only to other basal ganglia components.

nodes.rationale: Autoreceptors sense the neuron's own transmitter and typically inhibit its further release or synthesis, so release is regulated by negative feedback.

nodes.rationale: TAAR1 and D2sh have opposite effects on protein kinase signaling, hence opposite effects on DAT phosphorylation and dopamine reuptake.

nodes.rationale: Two receptors with opposite effects on transporter function (D2 autoreceptor activates DAT, TAAR1 inactivates it) allow bidirectional regulation of the monoaminergic system.

nodes.norm_label: presynaptic ca2+ channel inhibition and k+ channel opening

nodes.norm_label: neuromodulatory effects on firing, bursting and synaptic efficacy

nodes.label: Volume transmission via cerebrospinal fluid
nodes.rationale: A neuromodulator behaves like a transmitter that is not reabsorbed or locally metabolized; it can linger in CSF and modulate many neurons at once.

nodes.label: Metabotropic GPCR second-messenger signaling
nodes.rationale: Neuromodulators bind GPCRs and trigger second messenger cascades giving broad, long-lasting signals that last hundreds of milliseconds to several minutes.

nodes.label: Blood-brain barrier
nodes.rationale: Barrier to chemicals dissolved in the blood, protecting the brain from most neurotoxins found in food.

nodes.label: Allocortex
nodes.rationale: Three/four-layered cortex making up the remaining ~10%.

nodes.label: Parasympathetic nervous system
nodes.rationale: Activated when the organism is in a relaxed state.

nodes.label: Sympathetic nervous system
nodes.rationale: Activated in emergencies to mobilize energy.

nodes.label: Neurovascular unit
nodes.rationale: Regulates cerebral blood flow to rapidly satisfy the high energy demands of activated neurons.

nodes.label: Endocrine system
nodes.rationale: Works in tandem with the nervous system to respond to environmental changes affecting the body.

nodes.label: Neural pathways, circuits and large-scale networks
nodes.norm_label: neural pathways, circuits and large-scale networks

nodes.label: Synapse (electrical and chemical)
nodes.rationale: Membrane-to-membrane junction allowing rapid electrical or chemical signal transmission; the defining property of neurons.

nodes.label: Bilaterian nervous system body plan
nodes.rationale: Common structure (brain, central cord, radiating nerves) that originated in the Ediacaran period over 550 million years ago.

nodes.label: Nerve net
nodes.rationale: Diffuse network of isolated cells found in radially symmetric animals such as cnidarians and ctenophores.

nodes.label: Microglia
nodes.rationale: Specialized macrophages involved in the brain's immune system and clearance of metabolites.

nodes.label: Olfactory epithelium
nodes.rationale: Only central nervous tissue outside the meninges in direct contact with the environment, opening a pathway for therapeutic agents that cannot otherwise cross the meninges barrier.

nodes.label: Gliosis
nodes.rationale: Astrocytes proliferate upon CNS injury, forming neuronal scar tissue that lacks functional neurons.

nodes.label: Somatosensory cortex
nodes.rationale: Reported thicker in migraine patients, though a larger later study found no change.

nodes.label: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
nodes.norm_label: magnetic resonance imaging of the brain

nodes.label: Neocortex (six-layered)
nodes.rationale: Makes up about 90% of the cerebral cortex.

nodes.label: Brain weight to cortical thickness scaling
nodes.norm_label: brain weight to cortical thickness scaling
nodes.rationale: Larger brains have thicker cortices with an approximately logarithmic relationship: about 0.5 mm in shrews versus 2-4 mm in humans and fin whales.

nodes.label: Microgyrus
nodes.rationale: Genetic disorder with decreased folding where cortex has four layers instead of six.

nodes.label: Gyrification (cortical folding)
nodes.rationale: Folding fits a large surface area of neural tissue into the confined neurocranium, minimises brain and cranial volume, and is crucial for brain circuitry and functional organisation; small-brained mammals have smooth cortex.

nodes.label: Thalamocortical radiations
nodes.rationale: Nerve fibers project from the thalamus to the cerebral cortex in all directions, allowing hub-like exchanges of information.

nodes.label: Thalamic reticular nucleus
nodes.rationale: Notable exception: unlike almost all thalamic neurons it does not project to the cerebral cortex; envelops the lateral thalamus.

nodes.label: Wilhelm His Sr.
nodes.rationale: Swiss embryologist who in 1893 first recognized the thalamus as the main product of the diencephalon.

nodes.label: Regulation of consciousness, sleep and alertness
nodes.norm_label: regulation of consciousness, sleep and alertness

nodes.label: Sensory and motor signal relay to cortex
nodes.norm_label: sensory and motor signal relay to cortex

nodes.label: Neothalamus
nodes.rationale: Phylogenetically newest, lateral part of the thalamus.

nodes.label: Action selection
nodes.rationale: Basal ganglia exert inhibitory influence on motor systems; release of this inhibition lets a motor system become active (behavior switching). Hypothesized to extend to selection of cognitive actions; modeled computationally.

nodes.label: Addictive drugs (cocaine, amphetamine, nicotine)
nodes.rationale: Thought to work by increasing the efficacy of the mesolimbic dopamine signal.

nodes.label: Limbic sector of the basal ganglia
nodes.norm_label: limbic sector of the basal ganglia

nodes.label: Huntington's disease
nodes.rationale: Primarily involves damage to the striatum.

nodes.label: Substantia nigra (SNc, SNr)
nodes.rationale: Source of the striatal dopamine input.

nodes.label: Cerebellar cortex (folia)
nodes.rationale: Thin continuous gray-matter layer tightly folded like an accordion; about 730 square cm packed into a small volume.

nodes.label: Deep cerebellar nuclei
nodes.rationale: Almost all output from the cerebellar cortex passes through these four nuclei embedded in the white matter.

nodes.label: Cerebellar granule cell
nodes.rationale: Their vast number gives the cerebellum more neurons than the rest of the brain combined while occupying only 10% of brain volume.

nodes.label: Superior cerebellar peduncle
nodes.rationale: Mainly an output to the cerebral cortex, carrying efferent fibers from the deep nuclei via thalamic nuclei to upper motor neurons.

nodes.label: Marr-Albus theory
nodes.rationale: Climbing fiber input acts as a teaching signal inducing long-lasting changes in parallel fiber synapse strength, explaining sensorimotor calibration; supported by long-term depression observations but still controversial.

nodes.label: Cerebellum to neocortex neuron ratio (about 3.6)
nodes.rationale: Ratio conserved across many mammalian species.

nodes.label: Middle cerebellar peduncle
nodes.rationale: Largest peduncle; receives all its input from the pontine nuclei, relaying input from the cerebral cortex.

nodes.label: Pons
nodes.rationale: All connections of the cerebellum with other parts of the brain travel through the pons.

nodes.label: Motor coordination
nodes.rationale: The cerebellum does not initiate movement; it integrates sensory and brain inputs to fine-tune precision and timing of motor activity.

nodes.label: Pain desensitization pathway
nodes.rationale: Stimulated periaqueductal gray activates the nucleus raphe magnus, which projects to the posterior grey column of the spinal cord and inhibits pain transmission

nodes.label: Rostral-caudal functional division
nodes.rationale: Rostral reticular lesions caused hypersomnia in cats while caudal lesions caused insomnia, suggesting the caudal portion inhibits the rostral portion

nodes.label: Prefrontal lobotomy
nodes.rationale: Limbic-prefrontal connection was surgically severed to treat severe emotional disorders; patients became passive and lacked motivation

nodes.label: Limbic lobe
nodes.rationale: Named from Latin limbus (border) because its cortical structures surround the boundary between the cerebral hemispheres and the brainstem

nodes.label: Left amygdala
nodes.rationale: Its earlier developmental peak is inferred to give infants the ability to detect danger, as it responds predominantly to fearful events and faces

nodes.label: Gating Variables (n, m, h)
nodes.rationale: Potassium conductance uses n^4 because squid giant axon potassium channels have four subunits that must all be open.

nodes.label: 1963 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine
nodes.norm_label: 1963 nobel prize in physiology or medicine

nodes.label: Hodgkin-Huxley Model
nodes.rationale: Treats each component of an excitable cell membrane as an electrical circuit element to explain the ionic mechanisms of action potential initiation and propagation.

nodes.label: Extracellular electrical stimulation
nodes.rationale: Modern neural interfaces stimulate extracellularly to avoid membrane puncturing, which can cause cell death and tissue damage; it is unclear how far electrical neuron models hold for this mode.

nodes.label: Extracellular measurement
nodes.rationale: Preferred because it is easier to obtain, robust and long-lasting, and reflects the dominant effect in regions with many similar cells.

nodes.label: Hodgkin–Huxley model
nodes.rationale: Set of nonlinear differential equations relating ionic currents across the membrane to membrane voltage, fitted to the squid giant axon; supported by spike shape, ion identity and spike speed evidence; 1963 Nobel Prize.

nodes.label: Natural stimulus or pharmacological input neuron models
nodes.norm_label: natural stimulus or pharmacological input neuron models
nodes.rationale: Map chemical concentrations or physical stimuli (light, sound, pressure) to the probability of a spike event rather than to an output voltage.

nodes.label: Non-spiking cells
nodes.rationale: Cochlear hair cells, retinal receptor cells and retinal bipolar cells do not spike, and glia are not neurons, so they fall outside the scope of spiking neuron models.

nodes.label: Pyramidal neuron
nodes.rationale: Up to 95% of neocortical neurons are excitatory pyramidal neurons, each receiving tens of thousands of inputs, which makes spiking neurons a major information-processing unit of the nervous system.

nodes.label: Conductance-based neuron model
nodes.rationale: Treats neurons as points and describes membrane voltage dynamics as a function of trans-membrane currents.

nodes.label: Integrate-and-fire model
nodes.rationale: Mathematically simpler model that significantly simplifies ion channel and membrane potential dynamics; first studied by Lapicque in 1907.

nodes.label: Cable equation
nodes.rationale: Second-order partial differential equation obtained by combining the Ohm's-law longitudinal current relation with membrane resistive and capacitive currents.

nodes.label: Longitudinal axoplasmic resistance
nodes.rationale: r_l = rho_l / (pi a^2): a larger cross-section offers more paths for charge, lowering axoplasmic resistance.

nodes.label: Membrane capacitance per unit length
nodes.rationale: c_m = C_m * 2 pi a: more membrane is available to store charge as circumference grows.

nodes.label: Membrane resistance per unit length
nodes.rationale: r_m = R_m / (2 pi a): a larger circumference gives more area for charge to escape, lowering resistance (likened to holes in a garden hose).

nodes.label: Steady-state exponential voltage decay
nodes.rationale: V_x = V_0 e^(-x/lambda), the steady-state solution of the cable equation.

nodes.label: William Thomson (Lord Kelvin)
nodes.rationale: Developed 1850s models of signal decay in submarine telegraph cables, the origin of cable theory.

nodes.label: A-beta fiber
nodes.rationale: 6-12 um, 33-75 m/s; type II afferents for cutaneous mechanoreceptors, mostly touch.

nodes.label: A-delta fiber
nodes.rationale: 1-5 um, thinly myelinated, 3-30 m/s; type III afferents carrying cold, pressure and acute pain; faster than C fibers but slower than other group A fibers.

nodes.label: A-alpha fiber
nodes.rationale: 13-20 um, 80-120 m/s; includes type Ia and Ib sensory fibers and motor fibers to extrafusal muscle fibers.

nodes.label: A-gamma fiber
nodes.rationale: 5-8 um, 4-24 m/s; motor fibers to intrafusal muscle fibers.

nodes.label: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology
nodes.norm_label: guyton and hall textbook of medical physiology

nodes.label: Signal detection theory
nodes.rationale: Questions whether a stimulus has an absolute perceived intensity independent of context.

nodes.label: Buchsbaum and Stevens (1971) Neural Events and Psychophysical Law
nodes.norm_label: buchsbaum and stevens (1971) neural events and psychophysical law

nodes.label: Staddon (1978) Theory of behavioral power functions
nodes.norm_label: staddon (1978) theory of behavioral power functions

nodes.label: Narens ratio-scaling axioms
nodes.rationale: Testable properties for ratio-scaled judgments: the multiplicative property (veridical number use) was rejected, while the commutativity property was sustained.

nodes.label: Mechanoreceptor
nodes.rationale: Cutaneous mechanoreceptors: slowly adapting type 1 (form, roughness), slowly adapting type 2 (stretch), rapidly adapting (slip), Pacinian (high-frequency vibration).

nodes.label: Thermoreceptor
nodes.rationale: Bulboid corpuscle (end-bulb of Krause) and Ruffini end organ detect temperatures above and below body temperature.

nodes.label: Labeled Line Principle
nodes.rationale: Hot and cold signals travel on separate sensory fiber subpopulations, so each receptor has its own line conveying a simple sensation.

nodes.label: Photoreceptor Cell
nodes.rationale: Five compartments: outer segment (light capture), inner segment (metabolism), connecting cilium (protein trafficking), nuclear region, synaptic region (glutamate release).

nodes.label: Chemoreceptor
nodes.rationale: Distance chemoreceptors (olfactory system, vomeronasal organ) sense gases; direct chemoreceptors (taste buds, aortic bodies) sense liquids.

nodes.label: Five Traditional Senses
nodes.rationale: Touch, taste, smell, vision and hearing, classified by Gautama Buddha and Aristotle; pain, balance and temperature are also widely accepted, and some animals have magnetoreception and electroreception.

nodes.label: Sensory Nervous System
nodes.rationale: Sense organs act as transducers converting physical-world data into neural signals that the brain interprets as perception; a sensory system = sensory neurons + neural pathways + brain regions for perception and interoception.

nodes.label: Sensory Receptor
nodes.rationale: Commonly grouped into four categories (chemo-, photo-, mechano-, thermoreceptors); all transduce a physical stimulus into an action potential carried by afferent neurons.

nodes.label: Rod Cell
nodes.rationale: Rod-to-cone ratio correlates with diurnal vs nocturnal lifestyle: about 20:1 in humans, about 1000:1 in the tawny owl.

nodes.label: Hair Cell
nodes.rationale: Mechanoelectrical transduction: deflection toward the tallest stereocilia opens Na+ channels, depolarization opens Ca2+ channels and releases neurotransmitter onto the auditory nerve.

nodes.label: Olfactory Sensory Neuron
nodes.rationale: Axons form the olfactory nerve and synapse directly onto the olfactory bulb, bypassing the brain stem and thalamus unlike other senses, with links to the limbic system.

nodes.label: Retinal Three-Neuron Chain
nodes.rationale: Photoreceptor -> bipolar cell -> ganglion cell is the most direct route for visual information; the first action potential arises in the retinal ganglion cell.

nodes.label: Opsin
nodes.rationale: Rod and cone opsins serve conscious vision; melanopsin RGCs feed the body clock and project to the pretectal olivary nucleus rather than the LGN.

nodes.label: Non-image-forming Visual Functions
nodes.rationale: Pupillary light reflex and circadian photoentrainment operate independently of conscious visual perception.

nodes.label: Visual Area V1
nodes.rationale: Edge detection for spatial organization at ~40 ms; global organization from ~100 ms after LGN/V2/V3 input.

nodes.label: Visual Area V2
nodes.rationale: Handles illusory contours, depth from left/right image comparison and foreground segmentation.

nodes.label: Visual Area V6
nodes.rationale: Analyzes object motion relative to background and houses the topographical map for vision; V6A connects to premotor arm areas.

nodes.label: Visual Pathway (Optic Pathway)
nodes.rationale: Divided at the lateral geniculate nucleus into anterior and posterior visual pathways.

nodes.label: Visual System
nodes.rationale: Functionally divided into the optical system (cornea, lens) and the neural system (retina, visual cortex); supports stereopsis, depth, motion, pattern and colour perception.

nodes.label: Spinal nerve numbering convention
nodes.rationale: C1 emerges between occipital bone and atlas, so cervical nerves are numbered by the vertebra below (C8 sits between C7 and T1); thoracic, lumbar and sacral nerves are numbered by the vertebra above.

nodes.label: Cranial nerve numbering convention
nodes.rationale: Roman numerals follow the order in which nerves emerge from the brain and brainstem, front to back.

nodes.label: Phrenic nerve
nodes.rationale: Arises from C3-C5 and supplies the thoracic diaphragm; spinal cord transection above C3 prevents spontaneous breathing.

nodes.rationale: Neuroendocrine neurons are large, form coherent terminal fields and their output is easily measured in blood, making them tractable models for studying neuronal secretion and neural coding.

nodes.rationale: Cortisol inhibits the hypothalamus and pituitary, reducing CRH and vasopressin secretion and POMC cleavage into ACTH, keeping stress hormone output self-limiting.

nodes.label: Chromaffin cells
nodes.rationale: Act as postganglionic fibers converting sympathetic electrical impulses into a circulating chemical messenger.

nodes.label: GABA-A receptor biphasic modulation
nodes.rationale: Cortisol acts as a positive allosteric modulator at 1-10 pM and a negative allosteric modulator at 10-1,000 nM.

nodes.label: Glycogenesis
nodes.rationale: Cortisol paradoxically promotes both gluconeogenesis and glycogenesis in the liver, so it is better viewed as stimulating hepatic glucose/glycogen turnover.

nodes.label: Lipolysis (acute) and lipogenesis (chronic)
nodes.rationale: Acute cortisol promotes lipolysis; chronic lipogenesis is indirect, because raised blood glucose stimulates insulin, which drives lipogenesis over longer time scales.

nodes.label: Proteolysis and muscle wasting
nodes.rationale: Proteolysis supplies glucogenic amino acids as feedstock for gluconeogenesis.

nodes.label: Zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex
nodes.norm_label: zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex

nodes.label: Th2 immune shift
nodes.rationale: Cortisol inhibits IL-12, IFN-gamma, IFN-alpha and TNF-alpha but upregulates IL-4, IL-10 and IL-13; this Th2 shift is believed to protect against over-activation of inflammation during infection.

nodes.label: Open-Angle Glaucoma
nodes.rationale: Epinephrine increases aqueous humor outflow from the eye, which lowers intraocular pressure.

nodes.label: Adrenaline Infusion for Preterm Infants
nodes.rationale: Proposed in place of standard inotropes for cardiovascularly compromised preterm infants; more trials are needed to confirm reduced morbidity and mortality.

nodes.label: Fight-or-Flight Response
nodes.rationale: Adrenaline raises muscle blood flow, cardiac output via the SA node, pupil dilation and blood sugar to prepare the body for action.

nodes.label: Positive Regulation of Behavioral Fear Response
nodes.norm_label: positive regulation of behavioral fear response

nodes.label: Proopiomelanocortin (POMC)
nodes.rationale: ACTH is cleaved from the POMC precursor, which also yields the MSHs, lipotropins, CLIP and beta-endorphin.

nodes.label: Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal (HPA) Axis
nodes.rationale: Stress-response cascade: hypothalamic CRH drives anterior pituitary ACTH release, which acts on the adrenal cortex.

nodes.label: Julius Caesar Aranzi
nodes.rationale: Likened the ridge first to a silkworm and then to a seahorse, giving the Latin name hippocampus

nodes.label: Long-term potentiation (LTP)
nodes.rationale: First discovered in the hippocampus; widely believed to be one of the main neural mechanisms by which memories are stored

nodes.label: Circular sulcus of insula (sulcus of Reil)
nodes.norm_label: circular sulcus of insula (sulcus of reil)

nodes.label: Speech motor control
nodes.rationale: Pure speech apraxia from insular lesions shows the insula is part of a circuit coordinating articulatory movements, distinct from the cognitive language circuit of Broca's area.

nodes.label: Thalamus (ventral medial and ventral posterior lateral nuclei)
nodes.norm_label: thalamus (ventral medial and ventral posterior lateral nuclei)

nodes.label: LC-related disorders (depression, panic disorder, PTSD, ADHD, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's)
nodes.norm_label: lc-related disorders (depression, panic disorder, ptsd, adhd, alzheimer's, parkinson's)

nodes.label: Pons (rostral, lateral floor of fourth ventricle)
nodes.norm_label: pons (rostral, lateral floor of fourth ventricle)

nodes.label: Stress response (sympathetic activation)
nodes.rationale: Stress activates the LC, which raises norepinephrine secretion to alter cognition via prefrontal cortex, raise motivation via nucleus accumbens, activate the HPA axis, and shift autonomic tone via the brainstem.

nodes.label: Circadian rhythm
nodes.rationale: Reciprocal feedback between the raphe nuclei and the SCN provides an adaptable yet stable basis for circadian rhythms.

nodes.label: Dahlstrom and Fuxe (1964) visualization of serotonin neurons
nodes.norm_label: dahlstrom and fuxe (1964) visualization of serotonin neurons

nodes.label: Taber et al. (1960) first systematic examination of the raphe nuclei
nodes.norm_label: taber et al. (1960) first systematic examination of the raphe nuclei

nodes.label: Amnesia and confabulation
nodes.rationale: Basal forebrain damage reduces brain acetylcholine, which supports neuronal plasticity and learning, which may explain resulting memory impairments.

nodes.label: Deep brain stimulation of the nucleus basalis
nodes.norm_label: deep brain stimulation of the nucleus basalis

nodes.norm_label: goard and dan (2009) basal forebrain activation enhances cortical coding of natural scenes

nodes.norm_label: ventral striatum and substantia nigra/ventral tegmental region

nodes.label: Ventral attention network
nodes.rationale: Inhibited during top-down focused attention, which may prevent goal-driven attention from being distracted by irrelevant stimuli.

nodes.label: Network disruption in neuropsychiatric disorders (depression, Alzheimer's, autism, schizophrenia, ADHD, bipolar)
nodes.norm_label: network disruption in neuropsychiatric disorders (depression, alzheimer's, autism, schizophrenia, adhd, bipolar)
