nodes.label: Uddin, Yeo and Spreng (2019) six core networks proposal
nodes.norm_label: uddin, yeo and spreng (2019) six core networks proposal

nodes.label: Evolution of neuronal electrical signaling
nodes.rationale: Molecular evidence places the origin of electric signaling 700-800 million years ago (Tonian); peptidergic secretory cells gained gene modules for post-synaptic scaffolds and ion channels, a key innovation for nervous systems.

nodes.label: Axon
nodes.rationale: Cable-like projection carrying nerve signals away from the soma; can reach over a meter in human motor neurons and branches to reach many targets.

nodes.label: Axon hillock
nodes.rationale: Has the greatest density of voltage-dependent sodium channels and the most negative threshold, making it the spike initiation zone.

nodes.label: Dendrite
nodes.rationale: Branching extensions forming a fractal dendritic tree where most input to the neuron arrives via dendritic spines.

nodes.label: All-or-none law
nodes.rationale: A large enough voltage change over a short interval yields a full action potential or none at all.

nodes.label: Lipid bilayer
nodes.rationale: Highly resistant to ion movement, so the membrane bilayer functions as an electrical insulator.

nodes.label: Resting potential
nodes.rationale: About -70 mV at the axon hillock of a typical neuron.

nodes.label: Threshold potential
nodes.rationale: About -55 mV; action potentials trigger when enough depolarization accumulates to reach it.

nodes.label: Voltage-gated calcium channel
nodes.rationale: Generates calcium-based action potentials that may last 100 ms or longer.

nodes.label: Voltage-gated ion channel
nodes.rationale: Membrane proteins switching between closed and open states as a function of transmembrane voltage; the drivers of action potentials.

nodes.label: Voltage-gated sodium channel
nodes.rationale: Generates sodium-based action potentials lasting under one millisecond.

nodes.label: Depolarization
nodes.rationale: Sodium influx makes the interior more positive, opening more channels in a positive-feedback explosion until all available channels are open.

nodes.label: Axonal initial segment
nodes.rationale: Part after the axon hillock, shown by recent studies to be the most excitable part of a neuron.

nodes.label: Group C nerve fiber (type IV)
nodes.rationale: Unmyelinated, 0.2-1.5 um, 0.5-2.0 m/s; nociceptors and warmth receptors.

nodes.label: Micromachined 3D electrode array
nodes.rationale: MEMS micro-tower arrays penetrate outer skin layers to reduce impedance, noise and improve spatial resolution compared with wet surface electrodes.

nodes.label: Needle electromyography (EMG)
nodes.rationale: Most important component of electrodiagnosis of motor neuron diseases, often detecting involvement before clinical evidence.

nodes.label: Nerve conduction study
nodes.rationale: Determines whether nerve damage is present and how severe it is.

nodes.label: Anthropometric factors in conduction velocity
nodes.rationale: Age, sex, temperature, height and hand size shift baseline values; modeling them raises electrodiagnostic sensitivity and specificity.

nodes.label: NCV formula
nodes.rationale: NCV = conduction distance / (proximal latency - distal latency); velocity is calculated, not directly measured.

nodes.label: Node of Ranvier
nodes.rationale: Short (~1 um) unmyelinated gaps where voltage-gated sodium channels are densely packed and the action potential is regenerated.

nodes.label: Saltatory conduction
nodes.rationale: Action potentials 'hop' between nodes of Ranvier instead of travelling as a continuous wave, markedly faster for axons above a certain diameter.

nodes.label: Multiple sclerosis
nodes.rationale: Best known demyelinating disorder due to its high prevalence; affects the central nervous system.

nodes.label: Schwann cell
nodes.rationale: PNS glial cell that myelinates only a section of one axon.

nodes.label: Oligodendrocyte
nodes.rationale: CNS glial cell whose foot processes myelinate multiple nearby axons.

nodes.label: Neuron doctrine
nodes.rationale: Neurons are discrete cells, not a continuous network, yet communicate with each other.

nodes.label: Chemical synapse
nodes.rationale: Presynaptic electrical activity opens voltage-gated calcium channels, triggering neurotransmitter release onto postsynaptic receptors; receptor signal transduction allows complex effects.

nodes.label: Electrical synapse
nodes.rationale: Gap junctions pass current directly without neurotransmitters; main advantage is rapid signal transfer, and coupling is bidirectional.

nodes.label: Mixed chemical-electrical synapse
nodes.rationale: Combines a fast electrical component with a slow chemical component.

nodes.label: Nitric oxide
nodes.rationale: Metabolic gas synthesized and released immediately after an action potential without vesicle storage.

nodes.label: Gliotransmission
nodes.rationale: Neuronal activity raises astrocytic calcium, releasing gliotransmitters (glutamate, ATP, D-serine) that regulate extracellular transmitter levels and synaptic transmission.

nodes.label: Neurotransmitter identification criteria
nodes.rationale: Synthesis in the neuron, release and response, experimental response on application, and a removal mechanism.

nodes.label: Otto Loewi
nodes.rationale: In 1921 showed via frog vagus nerve experiments that neurons communicate chemically; credited with discovering acetylcholine.

nodes.label: Reuptake
nodes.rationale: Transporters pump neurotransmitters back into axon terminals for storage and reuse.

nodes.label: Adrian-Zotterman 1926 Muscle Weight Experiment
nodes.rationale: Concluded that action potentials are unitary events and that event frequency, not magnitude, underlies inter-neuronal communication.

nodes.label: Graded Potential
nodes.rationale: Trade-off: higher information rate and fidelity than spiking, but the signal decays faster, requiring short inter-neuron distances and high neuronal density.

nodes.label: Rate Code
nodes.rationale: Assumes stimulus information is carried by firing rate and ignores spike timing, making it inefficient but highly robust to ISI noise; became standard partly because rates are easy to measure.

nodes.label: Spike-Count Rate (Average over Time)
nodes.rationale: Works for constant or slowly varying stimuli but discards temporal resolution; real-world input such as saccade-driven retinal images changes every few hundred milliseconds.

nodes.label: Neural Coding
nodes.rationale: Because action potentials are largely uniform regardless of stimulus or neuron type, frameworks describing how spike sequences encode information are treated as fundamental to neuroscience.

nodes.label: Hierarchical Receptive Field Theory
nodes.rationale: Simple receptive fields at lower levels combine into large complex fields at higher levels; later theorists added feedback from higher levels.

nodes.label: Mechanoreceptor Receptive Field Size
nodes.rationale: Large receptive fields detect change over wider areas but yield less precise perception, so fingertips use dense small fields (~10 mm2) while the back and legs use fewer large fields.

nodes.label: Horseshoe Crab Ommatidia Experiment (1956)
nodes.rationale: Limulus ommatidia were chosen because they function like human photoreceptors yet are much larger and easier to record.

nodes.label: Lateral Inhibition Across Abstract Dimensions
nodes.rationale: Inhibition between neurons adjacent in stimulus modality rather than space; thought to aid colour discrimination.

nodes.label: Lateral Inhibition
nodes.rationale: An excited neuron suppresses its neighbours, creating contrast in stimulation that sharpens sensory perception.

nodes.label: Neural Adaptation
nodes.rationale: Adaptation likely extends neurons' limited response range to encode signals with much larger dynamic ranges by shifting the range of stimulus amplitudes; it is stronger and more stimulus-specific at cortical than subcortical stages.

nodes.label: Active Inference
nodes.rationale: Motor actions are descending proprioceptive predictions; reflex arcs sample input to fulfil predictions, so perception and action form one inference machine.

nodes.label: Emulation Theory of Representation
nodes.rationale: Top-down and bottom-up signals are combined according to the expected noise in the sensory signal, so less trustworthy input gives predictions more weight.

nodes.label: McClelland and Rumelhart Parallel Processing Model
nodes.norm_label: mcclelland and rumelhart parallel processing model

nodes.label: Precision Weighting
nodes.rationale: Weighting prediction errors by estimated reliability (e.g. more confidence in daylight than at nightfall) is needed to minimise prediction error effectively.

nodes.label: Rao and Ballard Computational Model of Vision
nodes.norm_label: rao and ballard computational model of vision

nodes.label: Predictive Coding
nodes.rationale: Inverts the bottom-up view of perception: perception is constrained by prior predictions and sensory signals shape it only as prediction errors propagated up the cortical hierarchy; prediction errors serve both inference and learning.

nodes.label: Adams et al. (2013) Motor Cortex Review
nodes.norm_label: adams et al. (2013) motor cortex review

nodes.label: Cephalopod Non-inverted Retina
nodes.rationale: Photoreceptors in front with no blind spot; not homologous to the vertebrate retina (evolved separately); lacks an RPE analog so photoreceptors have shorter lifetimes.

nodes.label: Fovea Centralis
nodes.rationale: Avascular with minimal neural tissue in front of photoreceptors to minimize light scattering for high-acuity vision.

nodes.label: Muller Glia
nodes.rationale: Act as fibre-optic channels transporting photons to photoreceptors; elaborate the inner limiting membrane.

nodes.label: Retinal Photoreceptors (Rods and Cones)
nodes.rationale: Rods work in dim light giving monochromatic vision; cones work in bright light giving colour and high-acuity vision via a range of opsins.

nodes.label: APS Study on Inverted Retina Purpose
nodes.norm_label: aps study on inverted retina purpose

nodes.label: Inverted Vertebrate Retina
nodes.rationale: Explained either as an advantageous compromise or a maladaptive evolutionary relic; a third view says it aids photoreceptor maintenance and reduces light intensity (hagfish ancestry); glial cells channel green-red light to cones, enhancing daytime colour vision while scattering excess blue to rods.

nodes.label: Dorsal Stream (Where/How Pathway)
nodes.rationale: V1 -> V2 -> DM/V6 and MT/V5 -> posterior parietal cortex; motion, object location and visual guidance of saccades and reaching.

nodes.label: Line of Gennari
nodes.rationale: Stripe of myelinated LGN axons terminating in layer 4; gives the striate cortex its name.

nodes.label: Primary Visual Cortex (V1, Striate Cortex, Brodmann Area 17)
nodes.norm_label: primary visual cortex (v1, striate cortex, brodmann area 17)
nodes.rationale: Simplest, earliest cortical visual area around the calcarine fissure; about 140 million neurons per hemisphere with very high inter-individual volume variation.

nodes.label: Ventral Stream (What Pathway)
nodes.rationale: V1 -> V2 -> V4 -> inferior temporal cortex; form recognition, object representation and long-term memory.

nodes.label: Goodale-Milner Perception-Action Model
nodes.rationale: Ventral stream serves visual perception while dorsal stream mediates visual control of skilled action; supported by illusions distorting perceptual judgements but not grasping.

nodes.label: Visual Cortex
nodes.rationale: Each hemisphere processes the contralateral visual field; V1-V3 size varies three-fold, partly inherited.

nodes.label: Neuronal Tuning
nodes.rationale: Early areas have simple tuning (e.g. V1 responds to vertical stimuli); higher areas have complex tuning (e.g. IT neurons respond to specific faces).

nodes.label: Outer Hair Cells (Cochlear Amplifier)
nodes.rationale: Somatic and hair-bundle motors amplify traveling-wave amplitudes over 40-fold; three to four times as numerous as inner hair cells.

nodes.label: Inferior Colliculus
nodes.rationale: Multisensory integration implicated in the startle response and ocular reflexes; detects pitch via amplitude-modulation frequencies.

nodes.label: Middle Ear Ossicles (Malleus, Incus, Stapes)
nodes.rationale: Act as a lever amplifying pressure about 20-fold because the inner ear beyond the oval window is liquid-filled rather than air-filled.

nodes.label: Outer Ear
nodes.rationale: Auricle reflections give direction cues; the ear canal amplifies 3-12 kHz.

nodes.label: Auditory Cortex
nodes.rationale: Brings sound into awareness, identifies sounds and their origin; right side more tonality-sensitive, left side more sensitive to fine sequential differences.

nodes.label: Cochlear Nucleus
nodes.rationale: Bushy cells carry timing, stellate cells encode spectra, octopus cells decode timing, fusiform cells extract spectral location cues.

nodes.label: Superior Olivary Complex
nodes.rationale: First convergence of left and right cochlear signals; MSO uses interaural time differences and LSO interaural level differences to compute sound angle.

nodes.label: Basilar Membrane
nodes.rationale: Stiff partition supporting the organ of Corti that determines mechanical wave propagation along the cochlea.

nodes.label: Cochlear Sexual Dimorphism
nodes.rationale: Male/female differences in the spiral twist plus the cochlea's durability make it useful for sexing archaeological remains.

nodes.label: Endolymph
nodes.rationale: Potassium-rich fluid whose ionic difference from sodium-rich perilymph produces the electrical potential driving hair cells.

nodes.label: Helicotrema
nodes.rationale: Apex junction of vestibular and tympanic ducts; lets incompressible fluid pushed in at the oval window exit via the round window.

nodes.label: Inner Hair Cells
nodes.rationale: Single row of hair cells that provides the main neural output of the cochlea.

nodes.label: Organ of Corti
nodes.rationale: Sensory epithelium on the basilar membrane; hair cells are powered by the potential difference between perilymph and endolymph.

nodes.label: Middle Ear Pressure Coupling
nodes.rationale: Ossicles are needed because moving sound through a fluid-membrane system takes more pressure than air; the tympanic-to-oval-window area ratio raises pressure.

nodes.label: Outer Hair Cells
nodes.rationale: Three rows of hair cells that mainly receive neural input from the brain, modulating motility as the cochlea's mechanical pre-amplifier.

nodes.label: Auditory Cortex
nodes.rationale: Temporal-lobe region performing spectrotemporal analysis of input from the ear; required for conscious awareness of sound.

nodes.label: A1 Critical Period Plasticity
nodes.rationale: Early-life sound exposure (rat P11-13) persistently expands the A1 representation of that frequency; same exposure later causes no lasting change.

nodes.label: Tonotopy
nodes.rationale: Orderly frequency map in A1 mirroring the cochlea, where low frequencies map to the apex and high to the base.

nodes.label: Cortical Deafness
nodes.rationale: Bilateral destruction above the cochlear nucleus causes cortical deafness, whereas unilateral damage causes only slight hearing loss.

nodes.label: Sensory Homunculus
nodes.rationale: Pathways preserve stimulus location so neighboring cortical neurons represent nearby body locations, forming a somatotopic map.

nodes.label: Somatosensory System
nodes.rationale: Multimodal subset of the sensory nervous system for touch, temperature, pain, pressure and proprioception; split into mechanosensory and nociceptive subdivisions.

nodes.label: Lamellar (Pacinian) Corpuscle
nodes.rationale: Large isolatable corpuscle sensing 200-300 Hz vibration (optimum 250 Hz, matching textures under 200 micrometres).

nodes.label: Receptive Field
nodes.rationale: Small, dense SA1/RA1 receptive fields in fingertips and lips underlie fine texture, slip and flutter discrimination.

nodes.label: Generator Potential
nodes.rationale: Graded response to deformation; once threshold is reached, stimulus magnitude is encoded as impulse frequency.

nodes.label: Phasic and Tonic Receptor Adaptation
nodes.rationale: Phasic (rapidly adapting) receptors suit texture and vibration; tonic (slowly adapting) receptors suit temperature and proprioception.

nodes.label: Thalamus
nodes.rationale: Thought to bring pain into perception and act like a bouncer, letting certain pain intensities through to the cerebrum and rejecting others.

nodes.label: Nociceptive Threshold
nodes.rationale: Nociceptors fire only above a minimum intensity; threshold testing measures analgesic efficacy and dosing by tracking threshold elevation.

nodes.label: Parabrachial Area
nodes.rationale: Integrates taste and pain; if pain occurs at normal temperatures while the gustatory system is active, pain is attributed to poison.

nodes.label: International Association for the Study of Pain
nodes.norm_label: international association for the study of pain

nodes.label: Menthol
nodes.rationale: Activates TRPM8 in facial cold receptors with trigeminal axons, producing a freshness sensation that explains its use in toothpaste, shaving lotions and facial creams.

nodes.label: TRPM8
nodes.rationale: Mice lacking TRPM8 could not tell a warm platform from a cold one, indicating reliance on TRPM8 for cold sensing; it passes an inward cation current inversely proportional to temperature (about 10-35 C) and is also activated by menthol.

nodes.label: Zhang 2015 - Molecular sensors and modulators of thermoreception
nodes.norm_label: zhang 2015 - molecular sensors and modulators of thermoreception

nodes.label: Darian-Smith et al. 1979 - Warm fibers innervating palmar and digital skin of the monkey
nodes.norm_label: darian-smith et al. 1979 - warm fibers innervating palmar and digital skin of the monkey

nodes.label: Emergent Cold Receptor Hypothesis
nodes.rationale: A cold receptor is proposed to arise from the constellation of thermally sensitive proteins in one neuron (TRPM8, 2P-domain K+ leak channels, Na+/K+-ATPase, HCN channels, transient IKA) rather than from a single transducer.

nodes.label: Hypothalamic Thermoregulation
nodes.rationale: Pre-optic and hypothalamic temperature-sensitive neurons report core temperature; thermoreceptors enable feed-forward responses to predicted core temperature changes from environmental conditions.

nodes.label: Paradoxical Response to Heat
nodes.rationale: Some cold receptors fire a brief discharge above about 45 C; the responsible mechanism has not been determined.

nodes.label: Joint Receptors (Ruffini Endings and Pacinian Corpuscles)
nodes.norm_label: joint receptors (ruffini endings and pacinian corpuscles)

nodes.label: Golgi Tendon Organ Type Ib Afferents
nodes.norm_label: golgi tendon organ type ib afferents

nodes.label: Muscle Spindle Nonlinear Responses (Initial Bursts, History Dependence, Rate Relaxation)
nodes.norm_label: muscle spindle nonlinear responses (initial bursts, history dependence, rate relaxation)

nodes.label: PIEZO2
nodes.rationale: Nonselective cation channel underlying proprioceptor mechanosensitivity in mice; humans with PIEZO2 loss-of-function mutations show deficits in joint proprioception, vibration and touch discrimination.

nodes.label: Central Pattern Generator
nodes.rationale: Rhythmic activation persists in cats after removal of sensory afferents and the brain, showing spinal pattern generation; the spinal cord integrates proprioceptive input with descending commands and drives alpha and gamma motoneurons rhythmically.

nodes.label: Muscle Spindle
nodes.rationale: Stretch receptor within skeletal muscle that detects length change; runs in parallel with extrafusal fibers, unlike Golgi tendon organs which lie in series.

nodes.label: Muscle Spindle Macrophages (MSMPs)
nodes.rationale: Distinct macrophage populations suggest an immunological component in spindle maintenance; spindle density correlates with fascicle length and fiber velocity.

nodes.label: Nuclear Bag Fiber (Dynamic Bag1, Static Bag2)
nodes.norm_label: nuclear bag fiber (dynamic bag1, static bag2)

nodes.label: Alpha-Gamma Coactivation
nodes.rationale: Gamma motor neurons fire in parallel with alpha motor neurons to keep spindle afferents firing while extrafusal muscles shorten.

nodes.label: Fusimotor Sensitivity Modification
nodes.rationale: Gamma motor neurons do not add contraction force; acetylcholine release contracts intrafusal end portions, stretching the central region, opening stretch-sensitive channels and raising afferent stretch-sensitivity.

nodes.label: Fusimotor Set
nodes.rationale: Gamma activation scales with task novelty or difficulty: static gamma active in routine locomotion, dynamic gamma recruited in difficult tasks.

nodes.label: Fusimotor Template of Intended Movement
nodes.rationale: Static gamma activity acts as a temporal template of expected muscle length change; dynamic gamma sensitizes afferents to lengthening onset and trajectory deviations.

nodes.label: Goal-Directed Preparatory Fusimotor Control
nodes.rationale: Dynamic gamma activity is tuned during movement preparation, e.g. reducing Ia and stretch reflex sensitivity when the planned movement will stretch the spindle-bearing muscle.

nodes.label: Clasp-Knife Reflex
nodes.rationale: Before 1967 GTOs were thought to be high-threshold and to cause protective weightlifting failure via this reflex; that premise was shown incorrect.

nodes.label: Conway, Hultborn and Kiehn 1987 - Proprioceptive input resets central locomotor rhythm in the spinal cat
nodes.norm_label: conway, hultborn and kiehn 1987 - proprioceptive input resets central locomotor rhythm in the spinal cat

nodes.label: Prochazka, Gillard and Bennett 1997 - Positive Force Feedback Control of Muscles
nodes.norm_label: prochazka, gillard and bennett 1997 - positive force feedback control of muscles

nodes.label: Prochazka and Gorassini 1998 - Ensemble firing of muscle afferents during normal locomotion in cats
nodes.norm_label: prochazka and gorassini 1998 - ensemble firing of muscle afferents during normal locomotion in cats

nodes.label: Autogenic Excitation During Locomotion
nodes.rationale: During locomotion Ib input excites rather than inhibits motoneurons of the receptor-bearing muscle (positive force feedback) and affects stance-to-swing transition timing.

nodes.label: Muscle Force Encoding
nodes.rationale: Ib firing frequency encodes force of the associated fibers and population activity represents whole-muscle force across the entire physiological range, not only at high strain.

nodes.label: Cranial Nerve Nuclei III, IV and VI
nodes.norm_label: cranial nerve nuclei iii, iv and vi

nodes.label: Vestibulo-Ocular Reflex
nodes.rationale: Moves the eyes opposite to head movement to stabilize retinal images; works in darkness and is independent of visual input, and its impairment makes reading difficult.

nodes.label: Cupula Damped Oscillator Model
nodes.rationale: Cupula deflection follows alpha*s/((T1 s+1)(T2 s+1)) times head velocity; since T1 (about 5 ms) is much smaller than T2 (about 20 s), deflection is roughly proportional to head velocity over 0.1-10 Hz, which suits the VOR need for eye velocity opposite head velocity.

nodes.label: Amygdala (Olfactory Processing)
nodes.rationale: Processes pheromone, allomone and kairomone signals; this processing is secondary in humans due to cerebrum evolution and largely unnoticed.

nodes.label: Mitral Cells
nodes.rationale: Low firing rates and easily inhibited by neighbouring cells; mitral pulses to the hypothalamus promote or discourage feeding.

nodes.label: Olfactory Adaptation (Background Odor Suppression)
nodes.rationale: Odor mixtures are hard to decompose because each sensory neuron responds to multiple components; cortical feedback to the bulb is proposed to suppress the pre-existing background odor so a newly arrived foreground odor can be recognized.

nodes.label: Olfactory Timing Code
nodes.rationale: Odor concentration is determined from the time at which neuron clusters fire; the bulbar circuit transformation can be partly captured by a mathematical model.

nodes.label: Basic Tastes
nodes.rationale: Each basic taste brings either caution or craving depending on its effect on the body: sweetness identifies energy-rich foods, bitterness warns of poisons, savoriness encourages protein intake, salt supports ion and water homeostasis, and sourness warns of spoiled food and acids.

nodes.label: Saltiness
nodes.rationale: Salt is needed for ion and water homeostasis (e.g. passive water re-uptake in the mammalian kidney), so it elicits a pleasant taste at certain concentrations.

nodes.label: Savoriness (Umami)
nodes.rationale: Savory taste signals amino acids needed to build proteins, so it triggers a pleasurable response that encourages intake of peptides and proteins.

nodes.label: Sourness
nodes.rationale: Sour taste becomes unpleasant in larger quantities because it can signal rotten or spoiled food and acids that cause tissue damage.

nodes.label: John Newport Langley
nodes.rationale: His influential claim that the autonomic nervous system used only efferent (brain-to-body) signaling delayed interoception research for many years.

nodes.label: Visceroception
nodes.rationale: Narrower than interoception: limited to signals from the viscera (heart, lungs, stomach, bladder), excluding brain and skin.

nodes.label: Interoceptive Conditioning
nodes.rationale: Pavlovian conditioning experiments in dogs showed interoceptive sensations may be important for learned behavior and emotion.

nodes.label: Cuneate Fasciculus
nodes.rationale: Carries sensory information from the upper half of the body (nerves entering at or above T6); lies lateral to the gracile fasciculus.

nodes.label: Dorsal Column Nuclei (Gracile and Cuneate Nuclei)
nodes.norm_label: dorsal column nuclei (gracile and cuneate nuclei)

nodes.label: Gracile Fasciculus
nodes.rationale: Carries sensory information from the lower half of the body (nerves entering below T6); lies medial to the cuneate fasciculus.

nodes.label: Three-Neuron Ascending Relay (First, Second, Third-Order Neurons)
nodes.norm_label: three-neuron ascending relay (first, second, third-order neurons)
nodes.rationale: Ascending tracts typically use three levels of neurons to relay information from the point of reception to the point of interpretation in the brain.

nodes.label: Spinothalamic Tract
nodes.rationale: Decussates at the level of the spinal cord (usually 1-2 segments above entry via the anterior white commissure), rather than in the brainstem like the DCML pathway and lateral corticospinal tract.

nodes.label: Brodmann Areas 3, 1 and 2
nodes.rationale: Kaas suggested that, for homogeny with other sensory fields, only area 3 should be called primary somatosensory cortex because it receives the bulk of the thalamocortical projections.

nodes.label: Cervical Nerves (8; C1 Lacks a Dermatome)
nodes.norm_label: cervical nerves (8; c1 lacks a dermatome)

nodes.label: Dermatome Key Sensory Points and Anatomical Landmarks

nodes.label: Referred Pain
nodes.rationale: Visceral afferents converge on the same spinal cord level as dermatomal fibres, so the CNS cannot tell viscera from body wall and projects the pain onto that segment's dermatome (e.g., heart pain felt in the left arm or jaw).

nodes.label: Dermatome (Anatomy)
nodes.rationale: Skin area supplied mainly by afferent fibres from the dorsal root of one spinal nerve; C1 has no dermatome, thoracoabdominal dermatomes stack like discs while limb dermatomes run longitudinally, and exact borders are individual like fingerprints.

nodes.label: Spinal Cord
nodes.rationale: Main pathway connecting the brain and peripheral nervous system; transmits motor signals from the motor cortex and sensory signals to the sensory cortex, and independently coordinates reflexes via reflex arcs.

nodes.label: Central Pattern Generators
nodes.rationale: Circuits of spinal interneurons that control motor instructions for rhythmic movements such as walking.

nodes.label: Pyramidal Tract Lesion
nodes.rationale: Lesions paralyze the corresponding side; patients relearn crude motions but not fine movement, implying the tract is crucial for fine movement and recovery is only partial.

nodes.label: Anterior Corticospinal Tract
nodes.rationale: Remaining ~10%; stays ipsilateral and decussates at the exiting spinal level; controls trunk, shoulder and neck muscles.

nodes.label: Betz Cells
nodes.rationale: Very large layer V pyramidal cells, only ~5% of spinal-projecting cells but fastest conduction (>70 m/s) from brain to spinal cord.

nodes.label: Corticospinal Tract
nodes.rationale: White matter pyramidal motor pathway from cerebral cortex to spinal lower motor neurons and interneurons; over one million neurons, myelinated in the first two years of life; also modulates sensory information via somatosensory cortex connections.

nodes.label: Posterior Limb of the Internal Capsule
nodes.norm_label: posterior limb of the internal capsule

nodes.label: Lateral Corticospinal Tract
nodes.rationale: About 90% of corticospinal connections; crosses the midline at the medulla and controls limbs and digits.

nodes.norm_label: kolb & whishaw (2009) fundamentals of human neuropsychology

nodes.label: Contralateral Motor Control (Decussation)
nodes.rationale: Because 75-80% of connections cross the midline at the medulla, each side of the brain controls muscles on the opposite side of the body.

nodes.label: Agranular Isocortex
nodes.rationale: Six-layered motor cortex with reduced layer IV and large corticospinal neurons in layer V.

nodes.label: Motor Cortex
nodes.rationale: Posterior frontal fields (BA4 and BA6) that plan, select and execute voluntary movement; modern work favors overlapping action-type representations over a strict point-to-point homunculus.

nodes.label: Primary Motor Cortex (M1)
nodes.rationale: Brodmann area 4 on the precentral gyrus, subdivided into 4a/4p; issues descending commands for fine motor control and force.

nodes.label: Supplementary Motor Area (SMA)
nodes.rationale: Medial area 6; initiates internally generated actions, sequencing and bimanual coordination; sends direct corticospinal projections.

nodes.label: Action-Type Motor Map
nodes.rationale: Extended microstimulation evokes coordinated multi-joint actions (defensive postures, reach-to-grasp), implying overlapping action maps rather than one-to-one muscle control.

nodes.label: Mirror-Neuron Responses
nodes.rationale: Macaque F5 neurons fire during both executing and observing a grasp; proposed to support action understanding and imitation, extent in humans debated.

nodes.label: Direct Cortico-Motoneuronal Connections
nodes.rationale: Thought to underlie fine finger control, whereas most corticospinal terminals contact spinal interneurons.

nodes.label: Deep Tendon Reflexes - The Precise Neurological Exam (NYU)
nodes.norm_label: deep tendon reflexes - the precise neurological exam (nyu)

nodes.label: Glycine-Mediated Antagonist Inhibition
nodes.rationale: Interneurons release glycine onto hamstring motor neurons; relaxing the antagonist lets the lower leg extend unopposed.

nodes.label: Polysynaptic Reflex
nodes.rationale: Interneurons between afferent and efferent signals allow processing or inhibition of the reflex within the brain.

nodes.label: Reflex Arc
nodes.rationale: Sensory neurons synapse in the spinal cord so motor neurons fire without the delay of routing through the brain; the brain analyzes the signal after the reflex.

nodes.label: Saladin (2015) Anatomy & Physiology: The Unity of Form and Function
nodes.norm_label: saladin (2015) anatomy & physiology: the unity of form and function

nodes.label: Reciprocal Innervation
nodes.rationale: Motor neurons excite flexors while inhibitory impulses go to extensors so flexion is not opposed.

nodes.label: Crossed Extensor Reflex
nodes.rationale: Contralateral motor neurons stabilize the uninjured side and shift the center of gravity to keep balance while the injured limb withdraws.

nodes.label: Nociceptive Flexion Reflex Threshold
nodes.rationale: Measured by EMG of biceps femoris during sural nerve stimulation; reflex onset matches reported pain onset and reflex strength tracks pain strength.

nodes.norm_label: andersen (1996) modulation of the human nociceptive withdrawal reflex

nodes.label: Medium/Long-Latency Stretch Reflex (Supraspinal Control)
nodes.rationale: Signal travels above the spinal cord before returning, so latency is longer.

nodes.label: Short-Latency Stretch Reflex (Spinal Control)
nodes.rationale: Signal returns from the same spinal segment it entered, the shortest path and fastest response.

nodes.label: Eldred, Granit & Merton (1953) Supraspinal Control of the Muscle Spindles
nodes.norm_label: eldred, granit & merton (1953) supraspinal control of the muscle spindles

nodes.label: Alpha-Gamma Co-activation
nodes.rationale: Keeps spindles taut during contraction so stretch-reflex sensitivity is preserved as fibers shorten; otherwise spindles go slack and the reflex stops working.

nodes.label: Nucleus Reticularis Pontis Caudalis (PnC)
nodes.rationale: Pontine neurons whose inhibition reduces startle by about 80-90%.

nodes.label: Acoustic Startle Reflex
nodes.rationale: Triggered by auditory stimuli above about 80 dB; the ear-to-PnC pathway has under 10 ms latency.

nodes.label: Startle Effect on Aircraft Pilots
nodes.rationale: 2005 University of Southern Queensland study found startle from life-threatening events degraded pilot performance in accidents; proposed more frequent exposure to unexpected critical events in training.

nodes.label: Startle Response
nodes.rationale: Largely unconscious defensive response to sudden or threatening stimuli, associated with negative affect; varies with emotional state, posture and motor preparation.

nodes.label: Lang, Bradley & Cuthbert (1990) Emotion, Attention, and the Startle Reflex
nodes.norm_label: lang, bradley & cuthbert (1990) emotion, attention, and the startle reflex

nodes.label: Startle Reflex
nodes.rationale: Brainstem reflex that protects vulnerable parts (back of the neck, eyes) and facilitates escape from sudden stimuli.

nodes.label: Startle Latency Cascade
nodes.rationale: Masseter ~14 ms, eyeblink 20-40 ms, head 60-120 ms, neck 75-121 ms, shoulder 100-121 ms, arms 125-195 ms, legs 145-395 ms, mirroring descending spread down the spinal cord.

nodes.label: Iris
nodes.rationale: Pupillary reflex is better thought of as an iris reflex: the iris sphincter and dilator muscles are the active elements, the pupil is a passive opening.

nodes.label: Mydriasis (Pupil Dilation)
nodes.rationale: In low light conditions a dilated pupil lets more light into the eye.

nodes.label: Pupillary Reflex Efferent Limb
nodes.rationale: Each afferent limb drives two efferent limbs (ipsilateral and contralateral), which explains why light in one eye constricts both pupils.

nodes.label: Eight-Segment Pupillary Pathway Schematic
nodes.rationale: Decomposing the pathway into eight numbered segments lets clinicians localize a lesion by elimination from light-reflex test results.

nodes.label: Pupillary Light Reflex
nodes.rationale: Regulates light entering the eye by adjusting pupil diameter to retinal luminance; light in one eye constricts both pupils; standard clinical examination tool.

nodes.label: Intrinsically Photosensitive Retinal Ganglion Cells (Melanopsin)
nodes.rationale: Project to the pretectal nucleus rather than the lateral geniculate nucleus; influence circadian rhythms as well as the pupillary light reflex.

nodes.label: Pupillary Reflex Brainstem Assessment
nodes.rationale: Tests integrity of sensory and motor eye function; abnormal reflex indicates optic nerve injury, oculomotor damage, brainstem lesion/death or depressant drugs such as barbiturates.

nodes.label: Gap Junctions in CPGs
nodes.rationale: Act as low-pass filters passing slow membrane fluctuations; blocking them reduces rhythmic activity and can abolish fictive locomotion.

nodes.label: Half-Center Oscillator (Reciprocal Inhibition)
nodes.rationale: Neurons not rhythmic alone produce alternating activity when coupled by mutual inhibition; core feature of locomotor CPGs.

nodes.label: Neuromodulation of CPGs
nodes.rationale: Three roles: modulation intrinsic to or required for activation; reconfigures CPG to produce different outputs; switches neurons between networks or fuses networks.

nodes.rationale: Older excitatory/inhibitory simplification was overturned by many exceptions; modern view: sympathetic is a quick mobilizing system, parasympathetic a slower dampening system, with exceptions.

nodes.norm_label: chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla
nodes.rationale: Act as a modified sympathetic ganglion: preganglionic neurons synapse directly on them and they release mainly epinephrine into the bloodstream, the exception to the two-neuron rule.

nodes.label: Long Preganglionic / Short Postganglionic Fibers
nodes.rationale: Parasympathetic ganglia lie in or near the target organ, so postganglionic fibers are short and release transmitter diffusely via varicosities, unlike sympathetic ganglia located far from targets.

nodes.rationale: Non-invasive surrogate marker of cardiac parasympathetic (vagal) tone at the sinoatrial node.

nodes.label: Inflammatory Reflex (Cholinergic Anti-Inflammatory)
nodes.rationale: Efferent vagal fibers dampen pro-inflammatory cytokine release through cholinergic signaling, modulating innate immunity.

nodes.label: Cholinergic Anti-Inflammatory Pathway
nodes.rationale: Provides a regulatory check on the innate immune response to invasion and injury, preventing damage from excessive cytokine production.

nodes.label: Vagus Nerve Stimulation
nodes.rationale: Electrical vagus stimulation prevented or reversed arthritis, colitis, sepsis, hemorrhagic shock and heart failure in experimental models; proposed as an implantable alternative to anti-cytokine drugs.

nodes.label: Hippocampal Neurogenesis
nodes.rationale: Autoimmune T cells and microglia support adult hippocampal neurogenesis, linking adaptive immunity to memory and learning.

nodes.label: Type 1 cytokines (cellular immunity)
nodes.rationale: Functional classification is more useful outside structural biology; type 1 and type 2 subsets tend to inhibit each other, and dysregulation of this balance is studied in autoimmune pathogenesis.

nodes.label: Cytokine pleiotropy and redundancy
nodes.rationale: Considerable redundancy and pleiotropism make the old lymphokine/interleukin/chemokine nomenclature obsolete; redundancy is a consequence of homologous receptors, so receptor-based classification is argued to be more clinically useful.

nodes.label: Cytokine versus hormone distinction
nodes.rationale: Cytokines circulate at picomolar levels that can rise 1000-fold during trauma or infection and come from widespread cell sources, whereas classic hormones circulate at nanomolar levels from discrete glands.

nodes.label: Major depressive disorder
nodes.rationale: Proposed to be a maladaptive manifestation of sickness behavior driven by abnormal circulating cytokines.

nodes.norm_label: sickness behavior as costly signal of need
nodes.rationale: High direct and opportunity costs (fever energy, inactivity, appetite loss) make sickness behavior a credible signal that motivates others to care for the sick individual.

nodes.label: Eyam hypothesis
nodes.rationale: Sickness behavior evolved mainly to protect kin from transmissible disease by limiting contacts, reducing environmental contamination and signalling poor health; promoted by kin selection.

nodes.label: Anorexia-driven iron restriction
nodes.rationale: Reduced food intake lowers gut iron availability, which would otherwise aid bacterial reproduction.

nodes.label: Hypothalamic temperature set point
nodes.rationale: The hypothalamus works like a thermostat: raising the set point drives heat generation and retention until body temperature matches it.

nodes.rationale: Peripheral tissues generate their own near-24-hour rhythms that dampen in isolation; the SCN maintains body-wide control by synchronizing them.

nodes.label: SCN temperature resistance
nodes.rationale: An intact mammalian SCN resists heat-pulse phase resetting while peripheral oscillators reset; in ectotherms such as the ruin lizard temperature does shift SCN oscillators.

nodes.rationale: Many systems and mechanisms interact to keep safe levels of substances such as sugar, iron and oxygen in the blood.

nodes.label: Neurological level of injury
nodes.rationale: Defined as the lowest level of full sensation and function; damage corresponds to spinal nerves at that level and below.

nodes.label: Primary and secondary injury
nodes.rationale: Primary injury is immediate cell death; secondary injury is biochemical cascades triggered by the original insult that cause further tissue damage for minutes to weeks.

nodes.label: Sacral sparing
nodes.rationale: Preserved sensation or function at S4-S5 (incl. voluntary external anal sphincter contraction) defines an incomplete injury because these nerves connect to the lowest region of the cord, indicating only partial cord damage.

nodes.label: Secondary injury pathways
nodes.rationale: Ischemic cascade, inflammation, edema, apoptosis and neurotransmitter imbalances.

nodes.label: VMH Dysfunction (Hypothalamic Obesity)
nodes.rationale: A disabled VMH ignores peripheral energy signals, suppressing sympathetic activity and stimulating vagal activity, which raises insulin and adipogenesis and produces a chronic positive energy balance.

nodes.label: Antrectomy with Billroth I/II Reconstruction
nodes.rationale: Combined with vagotomy in peptic ulcer disease to reduce the rate of recurrence.

nodes.label: Highly Selective Vagotomy (Parietal Cell / Proximal Gastric Vagotomy)
nodes.norm_label: highly selective vagotomy (parietal cell / proximal gastric vagotomy)
nodes.rationale: Denervates only the acid-secreting fundus and body while sparing the antrum and pylorus (nerve of Latarjet), so gastric emptying stays intact and no drainage procedure is needed.

nodes.label: Truncal Vagotomy
nodes.rationale: Divides the main vagal trunk and denervates the pylorus, so a pyloric drainage procedure is required; also denervates the liver, biliary tree, pancreas and small and large bowel.

nodes.label: Vagotomy as Obesity Therapy
nodes.rationale: Started in 1978 after obese PUD patients lost weight following truncal vagotomy; vagal lesions are thought to curb insulin hypersecretion that inhibits fat oxidation and promotes energy storage in adipocytes.

nodes.label: Vitamin B12 Deficiency
nodes.rationale: Vagotomy reduces gastric secretion and can impair intrinsic factor production, which is needed to absorb vitamin B12.

nodes.rationale: For occlusive arterial disease: L2 and L3 ganglia and the intervening trunk are removed while the L1 ganglion is left in place because it is responsible for ejaculation.

nodes.rationale: Acute complication of Hirschsprung's disease marked by sudden fever, abdominal distension, vomiting and bloody or explosive stools.
